internet.question: What does HTTP stand for?
internet.explanation: HTTP = HyperText Transfer Protocol. It is the application-layer protocol used by browsers and servers to exchange resources on the web.

internet.question: Which port does HTTPS use by default?
internet.explanation: HTTPS runs on port 443 by default. Plain HTTP uses port 80. The 's' in HTTPS adds TLS encryption on top of HTTP.

internet.question: What is the role of DNS?
options: Encrypts traffic between clients and servers
Translates domain names to IP addresses
internet.explanation: DNS (Domain Name System) is the internet's phone book — it resolves human-readable names like example.com to machine-routable IP addresses.

internet.question: Which HTTP status code means 'resource not found'?
internet.explanation: 404 Not Found indicates the requested resource doesn't exist on the server. 200 = OK, 301 = permanent redirect, 500 = server error.

internet.question: Which HTTP status code indicates a permanent redirect?
internet.explanation: 301 Moved Permanently tells clients (and search engines) the resource has a new permanent URL. 302 is a temporary redirect, 307 preserves the request method.

internet.question: What's the main difference between TCP and UDP?
options: TCP is connection-oriented and reliable; UDP is connectionless and best-effort
TCP is used only for video streaming
internet.explanation: TCP establishes a connection and guarantees ordered, reliable delivery (used for HTTP, SSH). UDP is fire-and-forget — fast but no delivery guarantees (used for DNS, video, gaming).

internet.question: Which HTTP method is idempotent and safe?
internet.explanation: GET is both safe (no side effects) and idempotent (calling repeatedly produces the same result). PUT and DELETE are idempotent but not safe; POST is neither.

internet.question: What happens first when you type a URL and press Enter?
options: The browser sends a TCP packet
The browser performs a DNS lookup to resolve the domain
The browser opens a TLS handshake
internet.explanation: Before any connection can happen, the browser must turn the domain into an IP address via DNS resolution (checking caches, then querying resolvers).

internet.question: What is CORS?
options: A method for caching CSS files
A browser security mechanism that controls cross-origin HTTP requests
internet.explanation: CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser-enforced policy that lets servers declare which other origins may read their responses, relaxing the same-origin policy in a controlled way.

internet.question: Which storage option is automatically sent with every same-origin HTTP request?
internet.explanation: Cookies are attached to every matching HTTP request automatically. localStorage/sessionStorage/IndexedDB are JavaScript-only and never auto-sent.

html.question: Which tag is used to define an unordered list?
html.explanation: <ul> creates an unordered (bulleted) list. <ol> is ordered (numbered). <li> is the list item inside either.

html.question: What is the purpose of the <!DOCTYPE html> declaration?
options: It tells the browser to render in standards mode
html.explanation: <!DOCTYPE html> triggers standards-mode rendering. Without it, browsers fall back to quirks mode, which mimics 1990s buggy behavior.

html.question: Which attribute on is required for accessibility?
html.explanation: alt provides a text alternative for screen readers and shows when the image fails to load. It's required by HTML and critical for accessibility.

html.question: Which is a semantic HTML5 element?
html.explanation: <article> is semantic — it conveys meaning (a self-contained piece of content). <div>/<span> are generic non-semantic containers.

html.question: What's the difference between <section> and <div>?
options: <section> implies a thematic grouping with semantic meaning; <div> is a generic container
html.explanation: <section> is a semantic landmark for related content (often with a heading). <div> has no semantic meaning and is used purely for styling/layout.

html.question: Which form method should be used for sending sensitive data?
html.explanation: POST sends data in the request body, not the URL — keeping it out of browser history, server logs, and referer headers. GET parameters are visible in the URL.

html.question: What does the <meta charset="UTF-8"> tag do?
options: Declares the character encoding so special characters render correctly
html.explanation: The charset meta tag tells the browser how to decode the bytes into text. UTF-8 supports virtually all written languages and is the modern default.

html.question: Which input type provides a built-in date picker in modern browsers?
html.explanation: <input type="date"> renders a native date picker in supporting browsers and validates the value as a YYYY-MM-DD string.

html.question: What is the purpose of the data-* attribute?
options: Stores custom data on an element accessible via JS dataset API
html.explanation: data-* attributes let you attach custom metadata to elements without breaking validation. They're readable in JavaScript via element.dataset.

html.question: Which is the difference between localStorage and sessionStorage?
options: localStorage is encrypted; sessionStorage is not
localStorage persists across browser sessions; sessionStorage is cleared when the tab closes
html.explanation: Both store key-value strings, but localStorage survives browser restarts while sessionStorage is wiped when the tab/window closes.

css.question: What does the CSS box model consist of (inside out)?
css.explanation: From the inside out: content area, then padding, then border, then margin. box-sizing: border-box makes width/height include padding+border.

css.question: Which selector has the highest specificity?
css.explanation: Specificity ranking (low→high): universal/type selectors → classes/attributes/pseudo-classes → IDs → inline styles → !important. IDs (#id) win over classes.

css.question: What does position: sticky do?
options: Behaves like relative until a scroll threshold is crossed, then becomes fixed
Locks element to the bottom of the page
Removes element from the document flow
css.explanation: Sticky elements scroll with the page until they reach a specified offset (e.g., top: 0), then 'stick' until their parent leaves the viewport.

css.question: Which Flexbox property controls how items grow to fill space?
css.explanation: flex-grow defines the proportion of free space a flex item takes. 0 means don't grow; 1 means fill available space; higher values take proportionally more.

css.question: What is the difference between :hover and ::before?
options: :hover is a pseudo-class (state); ::before is a pseudo-element (synthetic content)
css.explanation: Pseudo-classes (single colon) target a state of an existing element. Pseudo-elements (double colon) inject styled, synthetic content like ::before/::after.

css.question: Which property creates a new stacking context?
css.explanation: Setting z-index on a positioned (non-static) element creates a new stacking context. Other triggers include opacity < 1, transform, filter, and will-change.

css.question: What does `display: grid` do?
options: Lays children out in a one-dimensional row
Creates a two-dimensional grid layout system
css.explanation: CSS Grid is a 2D layout system — you can position items across rows AND columns. Flexbox, by contrast, is essentially 1D.

css.question: Which unit is relative to the root element's font size?
css.explanation: rem (root em) is always relative to the root <html> font size. em is relative to the parent. px is absolute. vh is viewport height.

css.question: What does !important do in CSS?
options: Overrides normal cascade and specificity for that property
css.explanation: !important raises the priority of a declaration above the normal cascade. Overuse breaks maintainability — use it sparingly, typically only for utility classes or third-party overrides.

css.question: Which CSS property is best for a smooth color change on hover?
css.explanation: transition interpolates between property values when they change (e.g., on :hover). animation is for keyframe-based, often-repeating motion.

javascript.question: What is the difference between let and var?
options: let is block-scoped and cannot be redeclared in the same scope; var is function-scoped and hoisted
javascript.explanation: let is block-scoped (constrained to {}). var is function-scoped and gets hoisted with an undefined initializer, which leads to subtle bugs.

javascript.question: Which comparison performs type coercion?
javascript.explanation: == (loose equality) coerces operands to a common type before comparing. === (strict equality) returns false if types differ. Always prefer ===.

javascript.question: What is a closure?
options: A function that has finished executing
A function bundled with references to its surrounding lexical scope
javascript.explanation: A closure is created every time a function is defined — it captures references to variables in its enclosing scope, allowing them to be used after the outer function has returned.

javascript.question: What does `typeof null` return?
javascript.explanation: typeof null returns 'object' — a famous, long-standing JavaScript bug preserved for backwards compatibility. Use `value === null` to test for null specifically.

javascript.question: What does `this` refer to inside an arrow function?
options: The this of the enclosing lexical scope
javascript.explanation: Arrow functions don't bind their own this. They inherit it lexically from the surrounding scope, which makes them ideal for callbacks.

javascript.question: Which is true about Promises?
options: They represent a future value and have states pending/fulfilled/rejected
javascript.explanation: A Promise is an object representing the eventual completion or failure of an async operation. Chained .then handlers run after the promise settles via the microtask queue.

javascript.question: What is the JavaScript event loop?
options: A loop that polls for user input
The mechanism that schedules tasks (callbacks, microtasks) onto the call stack
javascript.explanation: The event loop continuously checks the call stack and queues. When the stack is empty, it pulls the next microtask (Promise) or macrotask (setTimeout) and runs it.

javascript.question: What does the spread operator (...) do in `[...arr1, ...arr2]`?
options: Creates a new array with elements of arr1 followed by arr2
javascript.explanation: Spread expands an iterable into individual elements. Combined with array literals, it produces a new shallow-copied array — a clean alternative to concat.

javascript.question: What is hoisting?
options: Lifting a function out of a module
JavaScript's behavior of moving function and var declarations to the top of their scope before execution
javascript.explanation: During the compilation phase, JavaScript moves function and var declarations to the top of their scope. let/const are hoisted too but stay in the temporal dead zone until initialized.

javascript.question: What does Array.prototype.map return?
options: A new array of the same length with each element transformed by the callback
javascript.explanation: map returns a new array — same length as the source — where each element is the result of calling the callback. It does not mutate the original.

version-control.question: What's the difference between `git fetch` and `git pull`?
options: fetch downloads remote changes without merging; pull = fetch + merge
version-control.explanation: fetch updates your remote-tracking branches but doesn't touch your working tree. pull = fetch + merge (or rebase, with --rebase) into the current branch.

version-control.question: What does `git rebase` do compared to `git merge`?
options: Rewrites commits onto a new base, producing a linear history
version-control.explanation: Rebase reapplies your commits on top of another branch's tip, giving a clean linear history. Merge preserves the branching shape with a merge commit.

version-control.question: What's the difference between `git reset` and `git revert`?
options: reset moves the branch pointer (rewrites history); revert creates a new commit that undoes a previous one
revert is destructive; reset is safe
version-control.explanation: Use revert on shared/published branches — it's a forward-only undo. reset rewrites history and is safer only for local branches.

version-control.question: What is HEAD in Git?
options: A reference to the current commit/branch you have checked out
version-control.explanation: HEAD points to your current location in the repo — usually the tip of the checked-out branch. When detached, it points directly at a commit.

version-control.question: What does `git stash` do?
options: Saves uncommitted changes onto a temporary stack so you can switch context
version-control.explanation: stash saves your dirty working tree (and optionally untracked files) to a stack, leaving you with a clean working directory. Restore with `git stash pop`.

version-control.question: How do you copy a single commit from another branch?
version-control.explanation: cherry-pick replays one (or more) commits onto your current branch — useful for pulling a specific fix without merging the whole branch.

version-control.question: What does an interactive rebase (`git rebase -i`) let you do?
options: Reorder, squash, edit, drop, or reword commits in a range
version-control.explanation: Interactive rebase opens the commits in an editor where you can choose pick/squash/fixup/edit/drop/reword for each — a powerful tool for cleaning history before pushing.

version-control.question: What is the purpose of .gitignore?
options: Lists path patterns Git should not track
version-control.explanation: .gitignore lists files (build artifacts, secrets, node_modules) that Git should ignore. Already-tracked files must be removed with `git rm --cached` first.

version-control.question: After resolving merge conflicts, what's the next step?
options: Run git add on the resolved files, then git commit (or `--continue` if mid-rebase)
version-control.explanation: Editing files just resolves the text. You must `git add` the resolved files to mark them as resolved, then commit (for merge) or `git rebase --continue` (for rebase).

version-control.question: What is a fast-forward merge?
options: A merge where the branch tip can move directly to the new commit because there are no diverging commits
version-control.explanation: If the target branch has no new commits since the source diverged, Git can simply move the pointer forward — no merge commit needed. Pass --no-ff to force a merge commit.

vcs-hosting.question: What is a Pull Request (PR)?
options: A request to delete a branch
A proposal to merge a set of commits, with discussion and reviews, into a target branch
vcs-hosting.explanation: A PR (or MR on GitLab) packages your branch's changes for review. It's the unit of code review and CI verification before merging into main.

vcs-hosting.question: What's the difference between fork and clone?
options: Fork creates a server-side copy under your account; clone creates a local copy on your machine
vcs-hosting.explanation: Fork copies the repo into your account on the host (GitHub/GitLab) — useful for outside contributors. Clone downloads any repo to your local machine.

vcs-hosting.question: What do branch protection rules do?
options: Enforce policies (required reviews, status checks, no force-push) before changes can land
vcs-hosting.explanation: Branch protection prevents bypassing your workflow on critical branches like main: require reviews, passing CI, signed commits, linear history, etc.

vcs-hosting.question: What does the CODEOWNERS file do?
options: Maps file paths to required reviewers, auto-assigning them on PRs touching those paths
vcs-hosting.explanation: CODEOWNERS lets you say 'any change under /api/ requires review from @backend-team'. Combined with branch protection, it enforces accountability.

vcs-hosting.question: Which auth method is more convenient for CLI Git over the long term?
options: Personal access tokens via HTTPS — no per-push prompt
vcs-hosting.explanation: SSH keys (or HTTPS with a credential helper / PAT) avoid typing credentials on each push. GitHub deprecated password auth for Git operations in 2021.

vcs-hosting.question: What is GitHub Actions?
options: A CI/CD platform built into GitHub that runs workflows defined in .github/workflows/
vcs-hosting.explanation: GitHub Actions runs YAML-defined workflows on events (push, PR, schedule, etc.) — used for testing, building, deploying, and automating repository tasks.

vcs-hosting.question: What's the difference between 'Squash & merge' and 'Rebase & merge'?
options: Squash combines all PR commits into one; rebase replays them individually onto the base for a linear history
vcs-hosting.explanation: Squash gives a single tidy commit per PR. Rebase keeps each commit but lays them in a line — useful when individual commits are meaningful.

vcs-hosting.question: What's a tag in Git/GitHub?
options: A named, immutable pointer to a specific commit — typically used for releases (v1.2.0)
vcs-hosting.explanation: Tags pin a snapshot of the repo to a name. Annotated tags are full objects with author/message; lightweight tags are just refs to commits.

vcs-hosting.question: What is GitFlow?
options: A branching model with long-lived develop/release/hotfix branches alongside main
vcs-hosting.explanation: GitFlow defines specific branch types (feature, develop, release, hotfix, main). Modern teams more often use trunk-based development with short-lived branches.

vcs-hosting.question: What's the purpose of an issue tracker on GitHub/GitLab?
options: Capture, discuss, and triage bugs, features, and tasks linked to the codebase
vcs-hosting.explanation: Issues are the discussion unit for work items — linked to PRs, milestones, and projects. They keep planning, conversation, and code in one place.

package-managers.question: What's the difference between package.json and package-lock.json?
options: package.json declares ranges; package-lock.json pins exact resolved versions for reproducible installs
package-managers.explanation: package.json says 'I want react ^18.2.0'. package-lock.json says 'and exactly 18.2.0 with this exact dep tree'. Commit the lockfile.

package-managers.question: What does `npm ci` do differently from `npm install`?
options: Installs strictly from the lockfile, fails if it's out of sync, deletes node_modules first
package-managers.explanation: ci is built for CI environments — clean, reproducible, lockfile-strict. install can update the lockfile when ranges allow newer versions.

package-managers.question: In semver `^1.2.3`, which versions are allowed?
package-managers.explanation: Caret allows updates that don't change the leftmost non-zero digit — for ^1.2.3 that's anything <2.0.0. Tilde (~1.2.3) is stricter: <1.3.0.

package-managers.question: What are devDependencies?
options: Dependencies only loaded in dev mode at runtime
Packages needed only for development/build (not in production runtime)
package-managers.explanation: devDependencies (testing, bundlers, linters) are installed locally but typically excluded by `npm install --production` and not needed by consumers of your library.

package-managers.question: What does npx do?
options: Executes a binary from a package — installing it temporarily if not present
package-managers.explanation: npx runs commands from packages. If the binary isn't local, it fetches it temporarily — handy for one-off use of CLIs without polluting global installs.

package-managers.question: What problem do peerDependencies solve?
options: Declare a dependency the host must provide (e.g., react in a React plugin) to avoid duplicate copies
package-managers.explanation: If a plugin needs the same React copy as the host app, declaring react as a peerDep ensures one shared instance — preventing 'two reacts' bugs.

package-managers.question: Why does pnpm use a content-addressable store?
options: It hard-links each package version once and shares it across projects, saving disk and install time
package-managers.explanation: pnpm stores each version of a package once on disk, then hard-links into project node_modules. Result: huge disk savings and faster installs vs npm/yarn classic.

package-managers.question: What does `npm audit` do?
options: Checks installed packages against a vulnerability database and reports CVEs
package-managers.explanation: audit fetches advisories for your dependency tree and reports severity. `npm audit fix` attempts non-breaking upgrades; review carefully before applying.

package-managers.question: What is a workspaces feature?
options: A monorepo feature that hoists/links multiple packages in one repo for shared tooling
package-managers.explanation: Workspaces let you manage many packages in one repo (npm/yarn/pnpm all support it). Cross-package deps resolve via symlinks instead of registry lookups.

package-managers.question: What is the difference between dependencies and devDependencies in production builds?
options: Production installs typically only install dependencies; devDependencies are dev-time only
package-managers.explanation: When NODE_ENV=production or `npm install --production`, devDependencies are skipped. For frontend bundles, what's bundled depends on imports, not the dependency type.

pick-framework.question: What's the difference between a library and a framework?
options: You call a library; a framework calls you (inversion of control)
pick-framework.explanation: With a library (jQuery, lodash) your code drives. With a framework (Angular, Next.js) the framework owns the runtime and invokes your code at defined points.

pick-framework.question: What is the Virtual DOM?
options: A backup of the real DOM
An in-memory representation of UI used to diff and minimize real DOM updates
pick-framework.explanation: React (and others) build a lightweight tree, diff it against the previous tree, and apply only the necessary mutations to the real DOM — faster than re-rendering everything.

pick-framework.question: What's one-way vs two-way data binding?
options: One-way: data flows parent→child; two-way: data also flows back via events/v-model
pick-framework.explanation: React/Solid favor one-way (props down, events up) for predictability. Angular/Vue offer two-way binding (e.g., ngModel/v-model) for ergonomic forms.

pick-framework.question: What is JSX?
options: A syntax extension that lets you write HTML-like code that compiles to JS function calls
pick-framework.explanation: JSX (used by React, Solid, Preact) compiles to function calls like React.createElement(...). It's not HTML — it's syntactic sugar over JavaScript.

pick-framework.question: Why use a component-based architecture?
options: Encapsulation: reusable UI units with clear inputs/outputs that compose into apps
pick-framework.explanation: Components localize markup, behavior, and styles, making apps easier to reason about, test, and reuse — the dominant model in modern frontend.

pick-framework.question: What does 'reactivity' mean in Vue/Svelte/Solid?
options: Automatic UI updates when underlying state changes, tracked via signals/proxies
pick-framework.explanation: Reactive systems track which UI depends on which state. When state changes, only the affected UI re-runs — often without a Virtual DOM diff.

pick-framework.question: What is client-side routing?
options: JavaScript intercepts navigation and swaps views without a full page reload
pick-framework.explanation: SPAs use the History API to update the URL and render the next view in JS — keeping app state in memory and avoiding full reloads.

pick-framework.question: Which is a primary downside of a heavy SPA framework for content sites?
options: Larger JS bundles and slower first paint compared to server-rendered HTML
pick-framework.explanation: Big JS bundles delay interactivity and can hurt SEO/performance for content-heavy sites. SSR/SSG (Next.js, Astro) mitigate this.

pick-framework.question: What is hydration?
options: Attaching client-side event listeners and state to server-rendered HTML so it becomes interactive
pick-framework.explanation: After SSR sends HTML, the browser downloads the JS, then hydration walks the DOM and connects React/Vue state and event listeners — making it 'come alive'.

pick-framework.question: Why might a team pick Angular over React?
options: Angular ships an opinionated batteries-included framework (router, forms, DI, RxJS) — good for large enterprise teams
pick-framework.explanation: Angular gives one official answer for routing, forms, DI, HTTP, testing — useful when consistency across a big org matters more than ecosystem freedom.

writing-css.question: What does 'utility-first' mean in Tailwind CSS?
options: Compose UI from small single-purpose classes (p-4, flex, text-lg) instead of writing custom CSS first
writing-css.explanation: Utility-first inverts the traditional flow: instead of naming things and writing CSS, you compose pre-defined utility classes directly in markup, keeping styles colocated and consistent.

writing-css.question: What is Tailwind's JIT (Just-In-Time) mode?
options: On-demand class generation during build — only used utilities ship to the CSS file
writing-css.explanation: JIT scans your templates and generates exactly the utility classes used. Result: fast dev compiles and tiny production CSS regardless of how many utilities Tailwind 'has'.

writing-css.question: How do you use a custom value like a non-default color in Tailwind 3+?
options: Configure it in tailwind.config.js OR use arbitrary value syntax: bg-[#1da1f2]
writing-css.explanation: Either extend the theme in tailwind.config.js for reusable tokens, or use arbitrary values (`bg-[#1da1f2]`, `w-[37rem]`) for one-offs without leaving HTML.

writing-css.question: What does the @apply directive do?
options: Lets you compose Tailwind utilities into custom CSS classes
writing-css.explanation: Use @apply when a pattern repeats and a semantic class becomes clearer (e.g., .btn { @apply px-4 py-2 rounded bg-blue-600; }). Don't overuse it — it defeats the utility-first idea.

writing-css.question: Which Tailwind prefix targets medium screens and up?
writing-css.explanation: Tailwind is mobile-first: bare classes apply everywhere, and prefixes apply at the breakpoint and up. md: kicks in at 768px+ by default.

writing-css.question: How do you enable dark mode variants in Tailwind?
options: Configure darkMode: 'class' or 'media' in tailwind.config.js, then use dark: prefix
writing-css.explanation: With darkMode: 'class', adding 'dark' to <html> activates dark: utilities. With 'media', it follows the user's OS preference automatically.

writing-css.question: Why does Tailwind keep production CSS small?
options: Unused classes are purged via content scanning during build
writing-css.explanation: The build only generates the utilities found in your `content` glob. So even though Tailwind 'has' millions of possible classes, your bundle ships only what you used.

writing-css.question: What's a practical downside of utility-first CSS?
options: Markup can become noisy with many class names; needs componentization or @apply for repeated patterns
writing-css.explanation: Long class strings hurt readability — the standard fix is to extract repeated patterns into components (or @apply rules), not to revert to BEM globally.

writing-css.question: Which pseudo-class prefix in Tailwind targets focused state?
writing-css.explanation: focus: applies utilities when the element is focused (e.g., focus:ring-2). focus-visible: targets keyboard-only focus, which is better for accessibility.

writing-css.question: What's a common alternative to Tailwind for component-level styles?
options: CSS Modules / styled-components / vanilla-extract / scoped <style> in single-file components
writing-css.explanation: CSS Modules, CSS-in-JS, and SFC scoped styles all solve the global-leak problem differently. Tailwind solves it by avoiding custom names entirely.

css-architecture.question: What does BEM stand for?
css-architecture.explanation: BEM = Block (component), Element (a part of the block), Modifier (a state/variant). Naming convention: .card__title--large.

css-architecture.question: Why does BEM use long, hyphenated class names?
options: Long names act as flat, low-specificity, globally unique selectors — predictable and easy to override
css-architecture.explanation: BEM trades verbosity for predictability: every component lives at the same single-class specificity, no nesting, no surprises during overrides.

css-architecture.question: What's a key principle of OOCSS?
options: Separate structure (layout) from skin (visual styling) so they can be combined independently
css-architecture.explanation: OOCSS (Nicole Sullivan): separate structure/skin and container/content so styles compose. Bootstrap-style .btn + .btn-primary is a direct application.

css-architecture.question: What does ITCSS organize?
options: CSS into specificity-ordered layers: settings, tools, generic, elements, objects, components, utilities
css-architecture.explanation: ITCSS (Inverted Triangle CSS) layers go from broad/low-specificity to narrow/high-specificity, controlling the cascade so later layers win predictably.

css-architecture.question: What problem do CSS Modules solve?
options: Class-name collisions by scoping classes locally and exporting hashed names
css-architecture.explanation: Import styles from a module; the build hashes class names so .button in one file can't clash with .button in another. Truly local scope without naming gymnastics.

css-architecture.question: Which is true about specificity in scalable CSS?
options: Keep specificity low and consistent so overriding stays simple
css-architecture.explanation: Architectures like BEM, ITCSS, and utility-first all aim for flat, low specificity. The moment you need !important to win, you've usually lost the cascade battle.

css-architecture.question: What does 'co-located styles' mean?
options: Styles live next to (or inside) the component they style — improving discoverability and maintainability
css-architecture.explanation: Co-location (CSS Modules, styled-components, SFC <style>, Tailwind classes in JSX) puts styling next to behavior, so changing a component touches one place.

css-architecture.question: What is SMACSS?
options: Scalable and Modular Architecture for CSS — categorizes rules: base, layout, module, state, theme
css-architecture.explanation: SMACSS (Jonathan Snook) groups rules by purpose. It predates BEM but solves overlapping problems — scalability through deliberate categorization.

css-architecture.question: What's a major downside of deeply nested selectors (`.nav .list .item a`)?
options: High specificity makes overrides difficult and couples HTML structure to CSS
css-architecture.explanation: Each level adds specificity. Deep nesting locks the HTML shape into the CSS, so refactors break visuals — keep selectors short and flat.

css-architecture.question: What's the modern argument against BEM?
options: Component scoping (CSS Modules, scoped styles, utility classes) makes the verbose naming convention unnecessary
css-architecture.explanation: BEM solves global-namespace collisions in plain CSS. When the build (CSS Modules, SFCs, Tailwind) already scopes styles, BEM's verbosity often outweighs its benefit.

css-preprocessors.question: Which is a feature of Sass that vanilla CSS lacked until recently?
options: Variables, nesting, mixins, functions, partials, math operators
css-preprocessors.explanation: Native CSS now has variables and (newer) nesting, but Sass added these — plus mixins, @each, math, and partial imports — long before the platform did.

css-preprocessors.question: What's the difference between @mixin/@include and @extend?
options: @mixin reuses code blocks (with optional arguments); @extend shares the same selector list, generating no duplicate rules
css-preprocessors.explanation: @include duplicates declarations (good for parameterized output). @extend groups selectors at the rule itself (zero declaration duplication, but harder to predict output).

css-preprocessors.question: What is a Sass partial?
options: A file beginning with _ that's meant to be @use'd or @import'ed and not compiled standalone
css-preprocessors.explanation: Filename starting with underscore (_buttons.scss) tells Sass: don't emit a separate CSS file for this; it's a chunk consumed by another stylesheet.

css-preprocessors.question: What's the difference between SCSS and Sass syntax?
options: SCSS uses braces and semicolons (CSS-superset); Sass uses indentation, no braces
css-preprocessors.explanation: Both compile to CSS. SCSS (.scss) feels like CSS with extra features; Sass (.sass) uses Pythonic indentation. Most teams pick SCSS for familiarity.

css-preprocessors.question: What does the & selector do in Sass?
options: References the parent selector inside a nested rule
css-preprocessors.explanation: Inside a nested rule, & is the parent selector. Useful for &:hover, &.active, or BEM-style &__element compositions.

css-preprocessors.question: What is PostCSS?
options: A tool for transforming CSS with JavaScript plugins (autoprefixer, nesting, modern features)
css-preprocessors.explanation: PostCSS isn't a preprocessor itself — it's a CSS-to-AST pipeline plus plugins. Common plugins: autoprefixer, postcss-preset-env, cssnano, tailwindcss.

css-preprocessors.question: What does Autoprefixer do?
options: Adds vendor prefixes (-webkit-, -moz-) to CSS based on Browserslist targets
css-preprocessors.explanation: Autoprefixer reads your CSS and inserts vendor prefixes only where needed for the browsers you target — saving you from writing/maintaining them by hand.

css-preprocessors.question: Why might deep Sass nesting be discouraged?
options: It produces deeply specific selectors that are hard to override and tightly couple CSS to HTML
css-preprocessors.explanation: Each nest adds to specificity and creates compound selectors. Common rule of thumb: don't go deeper than 2-3 levels; flatten via BEM-like patterns instead.

css-preprocessors.question: What's @use vs @import in Sass?
options: @use namespaces members and avoids duplication; @import is legacy and dumps everything globally
css-preprocessors.explanation: Modern Sass replaced @import with @use (modules) and @forward. @use scopes variables/mixins to the file, preventing global pollution and accidental shadowing.

css-preprocessors.question: What is a Sass map?
options: A key-value collection, accessed with map.get(), useful for theme tokens
css-preprocessors.explanation: Maps store related tokens like (small: 4px, medium: 8px, large: 16px). Iterate with @each to generate utility classes from a single source of truth.

linters-formatters.question: What problem does ESLint primarily solve?
options: Statically detects bug-prone or inconsistent code patterns based on rules
linters-formatters.explanation: ESLint analyzes JS/TS via AST and flags rule violations (unused vars, no-console, react-hooks deps). It can be opinionated about style too, but Prettier is usually preferred for that.

linters-formatters.question: What's the difference between ESLint and Prettier?
options: ESLint catches code-quality issues; Prettier reformats code to a consistent style
linters-formatters.explanation: Prettier handles formatting (whitespace, quotes, line length). ESLint handles code quality. Use eslint-config-prettier to disable ESLint's stylistic rules so they don't fight.

linters-formatters.question: What does eslint-config-prettier do?
options: Disables ESLint formatting rules that conflict with Prettier
linters-formatters.explanation: Without it, ESLint and Prettier can disagree on the same line (single vs double quotes, trailing commas). The config turns off conflicting ESLint rules so Prettier wins.

linters-formatters.question: What does an ESLint rule severity of 'warn' (1) mean?
options: Logs a warning but doesn't fail the linter exit code
linters-formatters.explanation: Severity 0=off, 1=warn (no exit failure), 2=error (non-zero exit). CI typically runs with --max-warnings 0 to fail on warnings too.

linters-formatters.question: What does ESLint --fix do?
options: Automatically applies fixes for rules that support auto-fixing
linters-formatters.explanation: Many ESLint rules have an auto-fixer (e.g., 'prefer-const' rewrites let → const safely). --fix runs them; review the diff before committing.

linters-formatters.question: Why pair Husky with lint-staged?
options: Run linting/formatting only on staged files via Git pre-commit hook — enforcing quality without slowing the whole repo down
linters-formatters.explanation: Husky installs Git hooks; lint-staged runs commands on the files in the index. Together: pre-commit only lints what's changing.

linters-formatters.question: What is a flat config in ESLint v9+?
options: A new config format (eslint.config.js) that's flat (array-based) and uses ES modules — replacing .eslintrc
linters-formatters.explanation: Flat config simplifies config layering (no extends inheritance magic). Ported configs use defineConfig and arrays of config objects with files globs.

linters-formatters.question: What does the .eslintignore file (legacy) do?
options: Lists path globs ESLint should skip
linters-formatters.explanation: Like .gitignore but for ESLint. Flat config replaces it with `ignores: [...]` inside eslint.config.js.

linters-formatters.question: What does Prettier's printWidth control?
options: Preferred line length used to decide where to wrap code
linters-formatters.explanation: printWidth is a target (not a hard limit) for line length. Prettier wraps when reasonable; some constructs (long strings) may exceed it.

linters-formatters.question: Why might a team add a custom ESLint rule?
options: Encode project-specific patterns (e.g., disallow direct fetch, enforce import boundaries) that off-the-shelf rules don't cover
linters-formatters.explanation: Custom rules express team conventions as automatable feedback in PRs and editors — preventing entire categories of regressions you've already fixed once.

module-bundlers.question: Why do we bundle code at all?
options: Combine modules, transform syntax, and produce optimized assets browsers can load efficiently
module-bundlers.explanation: Bundlers resolve module graphs, transpile, code-split, tree-shake, and emit assets — letting devs use modern syntax/imports while shipping browser-friendly output.

module-bundlers.question: What is tree-shaking?
options: Eliminating unused exports from the final bundle by static analysis of ES modules
module-bundlers.explanation: Tree-shaking relies on ES module static structure. The bundler determines which exports are referenced and drops the rest, shrinking output.

module-bundlers.question: What does code splitting do?
options: Breaks the bundle into multiple chunks loaded on-demand (per route/feature)
module-bundlers.explanation: Dynamic import() boundaries become separate chunks. The browser only downloads what the current route needs, improving first-load performance.

module-bundlers.question: What's a Webpack loader vs plugin?
options: Loaders transform individual files (TS→JS, CSS→JS); plugins run during the broader compilation lifecycle
module-bundlers.explanation: Loaders are file-type transformers in the module pipeline. Plugins tap into compiler hooks for cross-cutting work (HTML emission, optimization, environment vars).

module-bundlers.question: Why is Vite typically faster in dev than Webpack?
options: Vite serves source files via native ESM during dev (no full bundle) and pre-bundles deps with esbuild
module-bundlers.explanation: In dev, Vite leverages browsers' native ESM and on-demand transforms. Production still bundles (Rollup), but dev-time HMR feels instant.

module-bundlers.question: What is a source map?
options: A mapping that lets browsers/devtools display original source code from minified output during debugging
module-bundlers.explanation: Without source maps, you'd debug minified one-liners. With them, devtools show your original TS/JSX, including correct line numbers.

module-bundlers.question: What's HMR (Hot Module Replacement)?
options: Swap updated modules into a running app in dev without full refresh — preserving state
module-bundlers.explanation: HMR is the productivity win of modern bundlers: edit a component, see it update in place without losing the open modal, scroll position, or form input.

module-bundlers.question: What's the difference between ESM and CommonJS?
options: ESM (import/export) is statically analyzable; CJS (require/module.exports) is dynamic and Node-historical
module-bundlers.explanation: ESM enables tree-shaking and top-level await thanks to its static structure. CJS requires runtime resolution and was Node's pre-ESM module system.

module-bundlers.question: What does dynamic import() return?
options: A Promise that resolves to the module namespace
module-bundlers.explanation: import('./foo') returns a Promise. Bundlers see this as a code-split point. Combined with React.lazy or Vue's defineAsyncComponent, you get on-demand loading.

module-bundlers.question: How do you analyze what's making your bundle big?
options: Read the minified file by hand
Use a bundle analyzer (webpack-bundle-analyzer, rollup-plugin-visualizer) to visualize module sizes
module-bundlers.explanation: Visualizers produce a treemap of bundle composition — quickly revealing accidental large deps (moment.js, lodash full import) and code-split boundaries.

testing.question: What's the difference between unit, integration, and end-to-end tests?
options: Unit: one function/component; integration: multiple units together; e2e: full user flow through the running app
testing.explanation: Each level tests bigger surface area. Pyramid: many unit, fewer integration, even fewer e2e — balancing confidence and speed.

testing.question: What is a mock function?
options: A test double that records calls and lets you stub return values, isolating the unit under test
testing.explanation: Mocks (jest.fn(), vi.fn()) let you assert how dependencies were called without invoking the real implementation — essential for testing in isolation.

testing.question: What is the Testing Library philosophy?
options: Test from the user's perspective — query by accessible role/text, avoid testing internal state
testing.explanation: RTL pushes you to interact with the UI like a user would. Resilient tests survive refactors as long as the user-visible behavior stays the same.

testing.question: What's a snapshot test good for?
options: Detecting unintended changes in serialized output (e.g., rendered markup) — fast feedback when something shifts
testing.explanation: Snapshots are best for stable output (small components, configs). They become noise if the output changes often or you blindly accept updates.

testing.question: Vitest vs Jest — what's the main appeal of Vitest?
options: Native ESM/TS support, Vite integration, fast startup, and a Jest-compatible API
testing.explanation: If you're already on Vite, Vitest reuses your config/transform pipeline — no separate Babel setup. Migration from Jest is mostly a name swap.

testing.question: What's the difference between Cypress and Playwright?
options: Both are e2e frameworks; Playwright has multi-browser support and runs out-of-process; Cypress has tight devtools/runner integration
testing.explanation: Both are excellent. Playwright's parallelism and cross-browser story (Chromium, Firefox, WebKit) is strong; Cypress's DX and time-travel debugger is loved.

testing.question: What does code coverage measure?
options: Lines/branches/functions/statements exercised by tests — not whether they're meaningfully tested
testing.explanation: Coverage is a useful smoke signal but not a quality measure: 100% line coverage with no assertions is meaningless. Use it to find untested code, not to claim safety.

testing.question: What is a flaky test?
options: A test that passes and fails non-deterministically, eroding trust in CI
testing.explanation: Flakes usually come from timing assumptions, shared state, or external services. Fix the root cause — disabling them just hides the problem.

testing.question: How do you test async behavior in Jest/Vitest?
options: Return/await the promise, use async test fns, or use waitFor for DOM-pending assertions
testing.explanation: Returning a promise (or using async/await) tells the runner to wait. For UI updates, use waitFor or findBy* from Testing Library which retry until the condition holds.

testing.question: What's TDD (Test-Driven Development)?
options: Red-Green-Refactor: write a failing test, make it pass, refactor — repeat
testing.explanation: TDD inverts the order. Tests drive the design. It works best when requirements are clear and feedback is fast — and stays valuable after the feature ships.

web-security.question: What is XSS?
options: Cross-Site Scripting — injecting malicious scripts into pages viewed by other users
web-security.explanation: XSS lets attackers run JS in a victim's session, potentially stealing tokens or impersonating them. Mitigate via output encoding, CSP, and avoiding innerHTML with untrusted input.

web-security.question: What is CSRF?
options: Cross-Site Request Forgery — tricking a logged-in user's browser into making unintended state-changing requests
web-security.explanation: CSRF abuses ambient credentials (cookies). Defenses: SameSite cookies, anti-CSRF tokens, requiring custom headers, double-submit cookies.

web-security.question: What does Content Security Policy (CSP) do?
options: Lets servers declare which sources of scripts/styles/images browsers should trust — blocking the rest
web-security.explanation: A strict CSP (no unsafe-inline, allow-listed origins) is one of the strongest XSS mitigations because injected scripts won't execute even if they slip in.

web-security.question: What does the SameSite cookie attribute do?
options: Controls whether cookies are sent on cross-site requests (Strict/Lax/None)
web-security.explanation: SameSite is the modern frontline CSRF defense. Strict/Lax means session cookies don't accompany cross-site form submits, breaking the attack.

web-security.question: What does the HttpOnly cookie flag do?
options: Prevents JavaScript (document.cookie) from reading the cookie — limits damage from XSS
web-security.explanation: HttpOnly stops XSS from exfiltrating the session cookie. Combine with Secure (HTTPS-only) and SameSite for hardened auth cookies.

web-security.question: What's the same-origin policy?
options: A browser rule that prevents JS from a different origin from reading another origin's responses
web-security.explanation: Origin = scheme + host + port. SOP is the bedrock of web security. CORS is the controlled mechanism to relax it for specific cross-origin requests.

web-security.question: Why is storing JWTs in localStorage risky?
options: It's accessible to any JS on the page — XSS can steal the token
web-security.explanation: JS-readable storage is XSS-exposed. HttpOnly cookies are safer for session credentials; if you must use localStorage, double down on CSP and input handling.

web-security.question: What's clickjacking and how is it prevented?
options: Tricking users into clicking on a hidden iframe of your site; prevented with X-Frame-Options or CSP frame-ancestors
web-security.explanation: Attackers overlay an invisible iframe of your site over decoy UI. Setting frame-ancestors 'none' (or 'self') blocks framing entirely.

web-security.question: What's an injection attack?
options: Untrusted input interpreted as code/queries — SQLi, command injection, NoSQLi, XSS, etc.
web-security.explanation: Defense: parameterize queries, use prepared statements, escape output for the right context, and never concatenate user input into commands or queries.

web-security.question: What's the OWASP Top 10?
options: A list of CVEs from this week
A widely cited industry list of the most critical web app security risks
web-security.explanation: Updated periodically by OWASP. Recent editions feature broken access control, cryptographic failures, injection, insecure design, security misconfiguration, etc.

auth-strategies.question: What's the difference between authentication and authorization?
options: AuthN: who you are; AuthZ: what you can do
auth-strategies.explanation: Identify the user, then decide what they're permitted to do. Modern systems often use OIDC for AuthN and OAuth2 scopes/roles for AuthZ.

auth-strategies.question: What is JWT?
options: JSON Web Token — a signed (not encrypted by default) token containing claims, used for stateless auth
auth-strategies.explanation: JWT = header.payload.signature, base64url-encoded. The signature lets servers verify integrity without a session lookup, enabling stateless auth across services.

auth-strategies.question: What's a refresh token used for?
options: Long-lived token kept securely; trades for a short-lived access token without re-authenticating
auth-strategies.explanation: Access tokens expire fast (minutes) to limit damage from theft. Refresh tokens (longer-lived, often rotated) renew them without prompting the user again.

auth-strategies.question: What is OAuth2 mainly designed for?
options: Delegated authorization — letting one app access resources on another with the user's permission
auth-strategies.explanation: OAuth2 issues access tokens after user consent (e.g., 'allow GitHub to read your gists'). It's about authorization. OpenID Connect adds authentication on top.

auth-strategies.question: What does PKCE add to OAuth2?
options: A code verifier/challenge that prevents authorization code interception in public clients
auth-strategies.explanation: PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) is now recommended for all OAuth flows — especially SPAs and mobile, where storing a client secret isn't safe.

auth-strategies.question: What's the safest place to store auth tokens in a browser app?
options: An HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie issued by the server
auth-strategies.explanation: JS can't read HttpOnly cookies, so XSS can't steal them. The browser sends them automatically — but you must guard against CSRF (SameSite + tokens or custom headers).

auth-strategies.question: What is SSO (Single Sign-On)?
options: A user logs in once with an identity provider and gains access to multiple connected apps
auth-strategies.explanation: SSO via SAML or OIDC centralizes login. Apps trust the IdP's assertion, so users authenticate once and roam between services.

auth-strategies.question: Why hash passwords with a slow algorithm like bcrypt/argon2?
options: Make brute-force attempts expensive even if the database leaks
auth-strategies.explanation: Fast hashes (MD5, SHA1) crack billions/sec on GPUs. Memory-hard, deliberately-slow algorithms force attackers to spend significant time per guess.

auth-strategies.question: What's the role of MFA?
options: Adds a second factor (TOTP, security key, push) so a stolen password isn't enough to log in
auth-strategies.explanation: MFA is one of the highest-leverage security wins. Hardware keys (FIDO2/WebAuthn) are phishing-resistant and the strongest second factor.

auth-strategies.question: What's the main appeal of stateless JWT auth?
options: Servers can verify signature without DB lookup, simplifying horizontal scaling
auth-strategies.explanation: Stateless = no server-side session store. Trade-off: revoking tokens before expiry is harder; many systems pair JWTs with short TTLs and refresh tokens or a deny-list.

type-checkers.question: What's the difference between `type` and `interface` in TypeScript?
options: interface can be re-opened/merged and extends ergonomically; type can express unions, intersections, mapped/conditional types
type-checkers.explanation: For object shapes they're largely interchangeable. Use interface when consumers might augment it (declaration merging); use type for unions, tuples, or complex compositions.

type-checkers.question: What's the difference between `any` and `unknown`?
options: any opts out of type checking; unknown is type-safe — must be narrowed before use
type-checkers.explanation: any is contagious — it disables checks on everything it touches. unknown forces you to check the type first (typeof, instanceof, type guards) before using it.

type-checkers.question: What are generics for?
options: Reusing logic across types while preserving type information (e.g., Array<T>, identity<T>)
type-checkers.explanation: Generics make functions/classes/types parameterized. function first<T>(arr: T[]): T returns the right element type instead of unknown.

type-checkers.question: What does Partial<T> do?
options: Makes all properties of T optional
type-checkers.explanation: Partial<{a: string, b: number}> = {a?: string; b?: number}. Common in update functions where only some fields change.

type-checkers.question: What's the difference between Pick<T, K> and Omit<T, K>?
options: Pick selects only the K properties; Omit removes the K properties from T
type-checkers.explanation: Use them to derive related shapes from a single source of truth, instead of duplicating types.

type-checkers.question: What is a discriminated union?
options: A union of object types sharing a literal 'tag' field, enabling exhaustive narrowing in switch/if statements
type-checkers.explanation: Add `kind: 'circle' | 'square'` to each variant; TS narrows other fields based on the kind in a switch. Combined with `never` checks, you get exhaustiveness.

type-checkers.question: What does `as` (type assertion) do?
options: Tells the compiler 'trust me, this value is type X' — no runtime effect
type-checkers.explanation: Assertions are an escape hatch. They don't validate at runtime — if you lie, you'll crash later. Prefer type guards or schema validation (zod) at boundaries.

type-checkers.question: What's strict mode in tsconfig?
options: Enables a bundle of strict flags (strictNullChecks, noImplicitAny, etc.) — recommended for new projects
type-checkers.explanation: `"strict": true` is the gold standard. It catches a wide range of bugs at compile time — null safety, untyped params, function variance, etc.

type-checkers.question: What does `readonly` modify?
options: Marks properties (or array/tuple) as immutable from TypeScript's perspective
type-checkers.explanation: readonly is compile-time only — JavaScript still allows mutation at runtime. Use it to communicate intent and catch accidental writes during development.

type-checkers.question: What does `keyof T` return?
options: A union of T's property names as string-literal types
type-checkers.explanation: For `T = {a: 1, b: 2}`, keyof T = 'a' | 'b'. Combined with mapped types and indexing (T[K]), it powers generic utilities like Pick and Record.

web-components.question: What are Web Components?
options: Browser-native standards (Custom Elements, Shadow DOM, HTML Templates) for building reusable encapsulated UI
web-components.explanation: Web Components are platform APIs — work without any framework. Frameworks can interop with them, and libraries like Lit make authoring them ergonomic.

web-components.question: What does customElements.define do?
options: Registers a new HTML tag (e.g., <my-card>) backed by a class extending HTMLElement
web-components.explanation: After registering, the browser instantiates your class wherever <my-card> appears in HTML and calls lifecycle hooks like connectedCallback.

web-components.question: What is the Shadow DOM?
options: An encapsulated DOM tree attached to a host element, with style and event scoping
web-components.explanation: Shadow DOM hides internal markup and styles from the outer document — your component's CSS won't leak out, and external CSS won't leak in.

web-components.question: What's the purpose of a <slot>?
options: A placeholder inside a component's shadow DOM where light DOM children get projected
web-components.explanation: Slots let consumers compose content into your component (think of <button>'s text being projected). Named slots support multiple insertion points.

web-components.question: Which lifecycle method runs when a custom element is added to the DOM?
web-components.explanation: Order: constructor (instance created) → connectedCallback (attached) → attributeChangedCallback (when observed attrs change) → disconnectedCallback (removed).

web-components.question: How do attribute changes flow into a Web Component?
options: Declare static get observedAttributes(); attributeChangedCallback(name, oldValue, newValue) fires when those change
web-components.explanation: Only attributes you list in observedAttributes trigger the callback — keeping it cheap. Convert string attrs to typed properties inside the callback.

web-components.question: What is the appeal of using Web Components in a multi-framework codebase?
options: They render in any framework — useful for shared design systems across React/Vue/Angular apps
web-components.explanation: Big orgs use them to ship one design system across teams that picked different frameworks. The platform is the lingua franca.

web-components.question: What's a downside of vanilla Web Components for app development?
options: They lack reactivity, templating, and SSR ergonomics that frameworks provide — Lit/Stencil close some gaps
web-components.explanation: Out of the box, you do manual DOM updates. Libraries like Lit add reactive properties and a templating system on top of the standards.

web-components.question: What does <template> do?
options: Holds inert markup parsed by the browser but not rendered until cloned into the DOM
web-components.explanation: <template> content is inert: scripts don't run, images don't load. Clone its content via cloneNode(true) to instantiate stamped DOM efficiently.

web-components.question: How do you style a Web Component from outside?
options: Through CSS custom properties, ::part(), and slotted content — encapsulation forces explicit style APIs
web-components.explanation: Encapsulation is the point — but components can opt-in to styling via CSS variables (theming) and ::part() (named internal elements). It's a design surface.

ssr.question: What's the main benefit of SSR vs CSR?
options: Faster meaningful first paint and better SEO because HTML arrives ready-to-display
ssr.explanation: SSR sends rendered HTML so users see content before JS loads, and crawlers index the actual content. CSR ships an empty shell that JS fills in.

ssr.question: What is hydration?
options: Attaching client-side React/Vue state and event listeners to existing server-rendered HTML
ssr.explanation: After the HTML loads, the framework walks the DOM, recreates the component tree in memory, and wires up listeners — turning static markup into an interactive app.

ssr.question: What is SSG (Static Site Generation)?
options: Pages rendered at build time and served as static HTML/assets — no server work per request
ssr.explanation: SSG (Next.js getStaticProps, Astro, Hugo) is great for content that doesn't change often: marketing, docs, blogs. Pair with CDN for blazing-fast delivery.

ssr.question: What does ISR do in Next.js?
options: Incremental Static Regeneration — re-renders specific static pages in the background after a TTL or on-demand
ssr.explanation: ISR combines SSG's speed with the freshness of SSR. Pages stay static but are revalidated at intervals or via API, so updates propagate without rebuilding the whole site.

ssr.question: What are React Server Components (RSC)?
options: Components that render only on the server, never ship JS, and can fetch data directly
ssr.explanation: RSC reduce client bundle size and enable secure server-side data access. They interleave with Client Components ('use client') for interactivity.

ssr.question: What's a hydration mismatch warning?
options: Server-rendered HTML differs from what the client renders during hydration — caused by non-deterministic code (Date.now, Math.random, locale)
ssr.explanation: React abandons mismatched DOM and re-renders client-side, hurting performance. Fix: stabilize server output or render the dynamic part in useEffect/Suspense.

ssr.question: What does streaming SSR enable?
options: Send HTML in chunks as parts of the page render — faster first byte and progressive interactivity
ssr.explanation: Instead of waiting for the entire page to render, the server flushes HTML as it's ready. With Suspense boundaries, the browser shows skeletons for slow areas while fast ones appear instantly.

ssr.question: App Router vs Pages Router in Next.js — what's a key difference?
options: App Router uses /app, supports React Server Components, layouts, and streaming; Pages Router (/pages) is the older file-based system
ssr.explanation: App Router is the future direction in Next.js 13+. Pages Router still works but new features land in App Router first (RSC, parallel routes, intercepting routes).

ssr.question: When would you choose CSR over SSR?
options: Internal dashboards or apps behind login where SEO doesn't matter and interactivity dominates
ssr.explanation: If users are authenticated and the app is highly stateful (canvas, IDE), the SSR overhead and hydration cost may not be worth it. Pure CSR can be simpler and adequate.

ssr.question: What is edge rendering?
options: Running SSR on edge runtimes (Cloudflare Workers, Vercel Edge) close to users for lower latency
ssr.explanation: Edge runs in many global locations. Trade-offs: faster TTFB, but the runtime is constrained (no native Node modules, smaller code limits) — use it for the right workloads.

graphql.question: What's the main difference between REST and GraphQL?
options: REST has multiple endpoints with fixed shapes; GraphQL exposes one endpoint and clients ask for exactly the fields they need
graphql.explanation: GraphQL gives clients precise control over the response shape, reducing over- and under-fetching. The trade-off is server complexity (resolvers, N+1 risk) and caching.

graphql.question: What's a Query vs a Mutation?
options: Query reads data; Mutation modifies data — both are typed in the schema
graphql.explanation: Queries are side-effect-free and parallelizable. Mutations are sequential by default (like POST/PUT). The convention separates intent and lets servers/clients optimize accordingly.

graphql.question: What's a resolver?
options: A function that returns the data for a specific field of a specific type
graphql.explanation: Each field has a resolver. The runtime walks the query, calling resolvers (often parents → children). Default resolvers usually just return obj[fieldName].

graphql.question: What is the N+1 problem?
options: Naive resolvers fetch a list (1 query) then a related field per item (N queries) — solved with DataLoader/batching
graphql.explanation: DataLoader batches and deduplicates per-request lookups. Without it, a list query of authors-with-books explodes into 1+N database queries.

graphql.question: What's a fragment?
options: Reusable selection set of fields, often per type — keeps queries DRY
graphql.explanation: fragment UserFields on User { id name avatar } can be embedded with ...UserFields wherever a User is selected — keeping field lists consistent across queries.

graphql.question: What does Apollo Client cache by default?
options: Normalizes query responses by __typename + id and serves matching fields from a normalized store
graphql.explanation: Normalized cache means a User updated by one query is reflected in all components reading that user — a big DX win, but requires correct __typename/id setup.

graphql.question: What are subscriptions?
options: A real-time GraphQL operation type — typically over WebSockets — for server-pushed updates
graphql.explanation: Subscriptions complement queries/mutations for live data (chat, notifications). They use WS or SSE under the hood and require infrastructure (pub/sub) on the server.

graphql.question: What's the purpose of persisted queries?
options: Send a hash instead of the query text — smaller payloads, registry-controlled queries, better security
graphql.explanation: Clients send a query hash; servers map it to a registered query. Reduces bandwidth and (with allow-listing) prevents arbitrary queries from clients.

graphql.question: When might REST be a better fit than GraphQL?
options: Public APIs with simple resource models, heavy caching needs (HTTP caching is easier), or small teams without schema discipline
graphql.explanation: REST plays beautifully with HTTP caching, CDNs, and tools. GraphQL shines for complex client-driven UIs with deeply related data.

graphql.question: What does the SDL look like?
options: A typed schema language: type Query { users: [User!]! } type User { id: ID! name: String! }
graphql.explanation: GraphQL's Schema Definition Language is human-readable. It's the contract between client and server, and powers tooling like codegen and introspection.

static-site-generators.question: When does an SSG render pages?
options: At build time, producing static HTML/CSS/JS files for deployment
static-site-generators.explanation: SSG (Astro, Eleventy, Hugo, Next SSG) prebuilds output. Result: zero server cost per request, perfect for content sites and docs at CDN scale.

static-site-generators.question: What's a key advantage of SSG over SSR?
options: Zero per-request server work and excellent CDN cacheability — fastest TTFB
static-site-generators.explanation: Static files cache forever at the edge. The cost is rebuild time on content updates — mitigated by ISR or incremental builds.

static-site-generators.question: What are Astro 'islands'?
options: Most of the page is static HTML; small interactive components hydrate independently — minimizing JS
static-site-generators.explanation: Islands architecture pushes the bulk of UI to zero-JS HTML, with interactivity scoped to specific components — ideal for content-heavy sites.

static-site-generators.question: When would SSR be better than SSG?
options: When content depends on per-request data (logged-in user, search query) or updates so frequently that prebuilding is impractical
static-site-generators.explanation: SSR personalizes per request. SSG can't easily do that — though hybrid approaches (Next.js, Astro) let you SSG most pages and SSR the dynamic ones.

static-site-generators.question: What's a headless CMS?
options: A content backend that exposes content via APIs — your SSG/framework handles rendering
static-site-generators.explanation: Decoupling content from presentation lets you use Sanity, Contentful, Strapi as the source while Astro/Next/Hugo render the front-end exactly how you want.

static-site-generators.question: What does 'incremental build' mean?
options: Rebuilding only the pages affected by a content change instead of the whole site
static-site-generators.explanation: Critical at scale (10k+ pages). Otherwise full rebuilds become slow. Tools/frameworks differ in how granular this is — check before committing.

static-site-generators.question: Why are SSGs particularly fast on a CDN?
options: Pre-rendered HTML can be cached at the edge with long TTLs — TTFB is essentially file lookup
static-site-generators.explanation: There's no origin compute per request. CDNs serve the file from RAM/SSD nearest the user. Cache invalidation triggers on deploy.

static-site-generators.question: What's a downside of pure SSG for a 100k-page site?
options: Build time grows with page count; full builds can take many minutes/hours without ISR or incremental builds
static-site-generators.explanation: Mitigations: ISR (Next.js), DPR/On-Demand Builders (Netlify), or page-level caching with revalidation. Pick a tool that addresses scale early.

static-site-generators.question: What's MDX?
options: Markdown with embedded JSX components — used in docs/blogs to mix prose and interactive UI
static-site-generators.explanation: MDX is huge in documentation sites. Write content in Markdown but drop in <Chart data={...} /> or <Tabs /> when needed — best of both worlds.

static-site-generators.question: What's hybrid rendering?
options: Mixing SSG, SSR, ISR, and CSR per-route in one app — common in Next.js/Astro/Nuxt
static-site-generators.explanation: Modern frameworks let you pick the right rendering mode per route: SSG for marketing, SSR for personalized pages, ISR for blog updates, CSR for interactive dashboards.

pwas.question: What three things minimally make a site a PWA?
options: Served over HTTPS, has a Web App Manifest, and registers a Service Worker
pwas.explanation: Add a manifest (icons, name, theme colors, display mode) and a service worker (offline/cache control), and serve over HTTPS — that's the baseline for PWA installability.

pwas.question: What's a Service Worker?
options: A scriptable network proxy that runs in the background, intercepting requests and enabling offline/caching
pwas.explanation: Service Workers sit between your page and the network. They can cache assets, serve offline, sync in background, and receive push notifications.

pwas.question: What's the Web App Manifest?
options: A JSON file describing the app (name, icons, start_url, display, theme_color) used for install prompts and the home-screen icon
pwas.explanation: Browsers read the manifest to enable Add to Home Screen and present the right metadata. Without it, install prompts don't appear.

pwas.question: What's a 'cache-first' strategy?
options: Service Worker checks cache first; falls back to network if missing — fast for static assets
pwas.explanation: Cache-first is best for assets that rarely change (fonts, images). Pair with versioned URLs or stale-while-revalidate to keep things fresh.

pwas.question: What's stale-while-revalidate?
options: Serve cached response immediately, then fetch in background to update the cache for next time
pwas.explanation: Great UX: instant response from cache while quietly updating in the background. Used heavily for content that's important to be fresh but not stale-blocking.

pwas.question: What enables offline functionality in a PWA?
options: A Service Worker that caches the app shell and required resources, plus a fetch handler that responds from cache when offline
pwas.explanation: The SW intercepts fetches. With cached HTML/CSS/JS and an offline fallback page, users get a working experience without network.

pwas.question: What's required to support push notifications in a PWA?
options: User permission, a Service Worker, and a push service (browser-vendor) endpoint to deliver messages
pwas.explanation: Browsers only deliver pushes via vendor push services. Your server sends the message to the endpoint; the SW receives it and shows the notification.

pwas.question: What does Lighthouse audit?
options: Performance, accessibility, best practices, SEO, PWA — gives actionable scores and tips
pwas.explanation: Run via Chrome DevTools or CI. The PWA category checks installability, manifest, service worker, HTTPS — a quick pass/fail to ensure you ship the basics.

pwas.question: What's background sync useful for?
options: Queue actions while offline (e.g., a posted comment) and replay them when connectivity returns
pwas.explanation: Background Sync (or Periodic Background Sync) gives PWAs reliability for transient network failures, replaying user actions when back online.

pwas.question: Why might a team still ship a native app over a PWA?
options: Deeper OS APIs (Bluetooth on iOS, advanced sensors), App Store distribution, or platform-specific UX expectations
pwas.explanation: PWAs cover most scenarios on Android. iOS PWA support has historically lagged (push, install UX), so apps with hardware-heavy needs may still go native.

mobile-apps.question: What's the main difference between React Native and Flutter?
options: RN renders native components via a JS bridge; Flutter ships its own rendering engine (Skia) and uses Dart
mobile-apps.explanation: RN feels native because it uses platform widgets. Flutter draws everything itself — pixel-perfect across platforms but not 'native' widgets.

mobile-apps.question: What's the React Native bridge?
options: Async JSON message channel between the JS thread and native modules — historically a perf bottleneck (replaced by JSI/Fabric)
mobile-apps.explanation: Modern RN's New Architecture (JSI, Fabric, TurboModules) removes the bridge serialization, enabling sync calls and a more responsive UI.

mobile-apps.question: What's the difference between Hot Reload and Hot Restart in Flutter?
options: Hot reload preserves state and patches Dart code in place; hot restart resets app state but reloads faster than a full rebuild
mobile-apps.explanation: Hot reload is the killer dev feature for iterating on UI without losing context. Hot restart helps when state has gone wrong but you want to skip the full toolchain.

mobile-apps.question: What's Expo for React Native?
options: A managed workflow with prebuilt native modules, OTA updates, and tooling — easier than a bare RN setup
mobile-apps.explanation: Expo lowers the entry barrier to RN: no Xcode/Android Studio for most apps, EAS Build/Submit, built-in modules (camera, location). Eject when you need custom native code.

mobile-apps.question: What's a native module in React Native?
options: Platform-specific code (Java/Kotlin or Obj-C/Swift) exposed to JS via a defined interface
mobile-apps.explanation: When JS APIs aren't enough (Bluetooth, deep platform integrations), native modules bridge to platform code. Newer JSI/TurboModules make this faster and type-safer.

mobile-apps.question: Why might Flutter feel more performant for animation?
options: It draws each frame itself via Skia/Impeller — no widget bridge — giving steady 60/120fps even with complex UIs
mobile-apps.explanation: Skia/Impeller (Flutter's graphics engines) provide consistent rendering across platforms. RN historically depended on platform UI behavior, which varied.

mobile-apps.question: What's the trade-off of Ionic compared to RN/Flutter?
options: Ionic uses a WebView (Capacitor/Cordova) — easy if you know web, but less native feel and potentially slower
mobile-apps.explanation: Ionic's appeal is leveraging existing web skills end-to-end. The web-in-a-shell model can hit performance/UX limits compared to RN/Flutter for high-fidelity apps.

mobile-apps.question: How do you handle platform-specific code in RN?
options: Platform.OS checks, .ios.tsx / .android.tsx file extensions, or native modules
mobile-apps.explanation: RN auto-resolves Foo.ios.tsx vs Foo.android.tsx by extension. Use Platform.select for small differences. Larger differences justify separate components.

mobile-apps.question: What's the typical bundle for a RN app?
options: A native iOS/Android binary that contains the JS bundle and runtime, plus compiled native code
mobile-apps.explanation: RN apps ship as platform binaries (.ipa, .apk/.aab). The JS bundle lives inside; OTA updates (CodePush, Expo Updates) can swap that bundle without re-submitting binaries.

mobile-apps.question: Why is React Native popular in many companies?
options: Reuse JS/React skills + much code across iOS/Android while still shipping native UIs — strong productivity per dollar
mobile-apps.explanation: RN's pitch: one team, one stack, two platforms. Big apps (Instagram, Discord, Shopify) ship hybrid native+RN to balance velocity and platform polish.

desktop-apps.question: What's Electron's architecture?
options: A main (Node.js) process spawning one or more renderer (Chromium) processes; communication via IPC
desktop-apps.explanation: Main owns lifecycle/native APIs/windows. Renderers run your web UI sandboxed (with appropriate flags). IPC (ipcMain/ipcRenderer) is how they talk.

desktop-apps.question: Why are Electron apps often large?
options: They bundle Chromium + Node.js — typically 100MB+ minimum disk footprint
desktop-apps.explanation: The full browser stack is the cost of using web tech for desktop. Code-signing, ASAR packaging, and prune-only-prod-deps mitigate disk size somewhat.

desktop-apps.question: What's Tauri's main appeal vs Electron?
options: Tiny apps (~3-10MB) by using the OS WebView and a Rust backend instead of bundling Chromium+Node
desktop-apps.explanation: Tauri uses platform WebViews (WebKit on macOS, WebView2 on Windows). Smaller, often faster, but you accept WebView differences across OSes.

desktop-apps.question: What does a preload script do in Electron?
options: Runs before page scripts in the renderer; the safe place to expose limited APIs via contextBridge to the web context
desktop-apps.explanation: Modern Electron security disables nodeIntegration and uses contextIsolation. Preload + contextBridge.exposeInMainWorld is the recommended way to expose Node APIs.

desktop-apps.question: Why is contextIsolation important?
options: It separates the preload Node context from the page's JS, preventing prototype pollution attacks from web content
desktop-apps.explanation: Without isolation, a compromised page could reach Node and execute arbitrary code on the user's machine. Always keep contextIsolation: true.

desktop-apps.question: What does code signing do for desktop apps?
options: Signs the binary with a developer certificate so the OS verifies authenticity and avoids warnings/blocks
desktop-apps.explanation: macOS Gatekeeper and Windows SmartScreen block or warn on unsigned binaries. Notarization (Apple) and EV certificates (Windows) further reduce friction.

desktop-apps.question: What is auto-update in Electron?
options: An update system (electron-updater + a feed) that downloads new releases in the background and prompts to restart
desktop-apps.explanation: Most apps use electron-updater talking to GitHub Releases or a custom feed. Differential updates and code-signing are essential for safety and bandwidth.

desktop-apps.question: What's IPC in Electron?
options: Inter-Process Communication — the API to message between main and renderer processes
desktop-apps.explanation: ipcMain/ipcRenderer (or invoke/handle for promises) move data and trigger actions across processes. Validate inputs at the main side — renderers may be compromised.

desktop-apps.question: Why might a team pick Electron over Tauri despite the size?
options: Mature ecosystem, Node.js access, consistent Chromium across OSes, and battle-tested apps (VS Code, Slack, Figma)
desktop-apps.explanation: Electron's stability and ecosystem are unmatched. Tauri trades size for OS WebView differences. Pick based on app needs and team comfort with Rust.

desktop-apps.question: How do you ship a native menu in Electron?
options: Use the Menu API to build a Menu from MenuItems and call Menu.setApplicationMenu
desktop-apps.explanation: Native menus integrate with macOS menubar and Windows window menus. Build them in main (where the Menu API lives), not the renderer.

what-is-javascript.question: Which best describes JavaScript?
options: A high-level, interpreted, dynamically-typed programming language for the web (and beyond)
what-is-javascript.explanation: JavaScript is dynamically typed, multi-paradigm (functional, OO, imperative). Despite the name, it's unrelated to Java — the name was marketing-driven in the mid-90s.

what-is-javascript.question: Where does JavaScript run today?
options: Browsers, Node.js, Deno, Bun, edge runtimes, embedded devices — virtually everywhere
what-is-javascript.explanation: JS engines (V8, SpiderMonkey, JavaScriptCore) ship in browsers, but also power servers (Node), edges (Cloudflare Workers), and even microcontrollers.

what-is-javascript.question: Who maintains the official spec of JavaScript?
