options: Ecma International (TC39 committee) — the spec is called ECMAScript
what-is-javascript.explanation: ECMAScript proposals advance through TC39 stages (0-4). 'JavaScript' is the popular name; 'ECMAScript' is the formal language spec.

what-is-javascript.question: Is JavaScript single-threaded?
options: Yes — single-threaded with an event loop; concurrency via async I/O and Web Workers
what-is-javascript.explanation: Each JS context has one main thread. Long work blocks UI/server. Web Workers, Worker Threads, and async I/O give parallelism without shared mutable state.

what-is-javascript.question: What's the relationship between JavaScript and TypeScript?
options: TypeScript is a typed superset of JavaScript that compiles to JS
what-is-javascript.explanation: All valid JS is valid TS. The TS compiler strips types and emits JS. TS gives compile-time safety; the runtime is still JavaScript.

what-is-javascript.question: Which engine powers Chrome and Node.js?
what-is-javascript.explanation: V8 (by Google) JIT-compiles JS for speed. Firefox uses SpiderMonkey, Safari uses JavaScriptCore. Bun and Deno also use V8 (Bun uses JavaScriptCore actually, Deno V8) — varies.

what-is-javascript.question: Which runtime feature does JavaScript NOT natively provide?
what-is-javascript.explanation: Browsers sandbox JS away from the FS. Node/Deno/Bun expose FS APIs server-side. Browsers offer the File System Access API only with explicit user permission.

what-is-javascript.question: What's the JavaScript execution model summary?
options: Single thread + event loop + microtask/macrotask queues
what-is-javascript.explanation: Synchronous code runs to completion. Microtasks (Promises) run between sync chunks; macrotasks (setTimeout, IO callbacks) wait for the next tick.

what-is-javascript.question: What's a key advantage of JavaScript for web development?
options: It's the only language that runs natively in every browser — full-stack JS unifies frontend and backend
what-is-javascript.explanation: JS's monopoly in browsers (until WebAssembly) made it inevitable. Sharing code/types between front and back (TypeScript + Node/Deno) is a productivity win.

what-is-javascript.question: Is JavaScript compiled or interpreted?
options: Just-In-Time (JIT) compiled by modern engines after profiling — feels interpreted but compiles hot paths
what-is-javascript.explanation: Modern engines parse, then interpret + profile. Hot functions are compiled to optimized machine code; deoptimized when assumptions break.

history-of-javascript.question: Who originally created JavaScript?
history-of-javascript.explanation: Brendan Eich wrote the first JavaScript prototype in 10 days at Netscape in May 1995. It was originally called Mocha, then LiveScript, then JavaScript.

history-of-javascript.question: Why was JavaScript named 'JavaScript' if it's not related to Java?
options: Marketing decision riding Java's hype in the mid-90s
It was a fork of Java
history-of-javascript.explanation: Java was the buzzword of 1995. Netscape struck a co-marketing deal with Sun and renamed LiveScript → JavaScript to leverage Java's popularity.

history-of-javascript.question: When did ES6 (ECMAScript 2015) ship?
options: 2015 — a major release with let/const, classes, modules, arrow functions, Promises
history-of-javascript.explanation: ES6/ES2015 was the largest single update in JS history, modernizing the language. After 2015, releases became annual (ES2016, ES2017, ...).

history-of-javascript.question: What was the 'Browser Wars' impact on JavaScript?
options: Netscape vs IE divergence led to inconsistent JS implementations and standardization via ECMAScript
history-of-javascript.explanation: Microsoft's JScript and Netscape's JavaScript drifted apart. ECMAScript standardization (1997) brought a common spec, eventually shared across all browsers.

history-of-javascript.question: What was AJAX, historically?
options: Asynchronous JavaScript And XML — using XMLHttpRequest to update parts of a page without reload (early 2000s)
history-of-javascript.explanation: Gmail and Google Maps popularized AJAX patterns in 2004-2005. It led directly to the SPA era and replaced full-page reload web apps.

history-of-javascript.question: When did Node.js launch?
options: 2009 by Ryan Dahl — bringing JS to the server with V8 + libuv
history-of-javascript.explanation: Node's event-loop, non-blocking I/O model made JS practical for servers. The npm registry (launched 2010) became the largest package ecosystem in the world.

history-of-javascript.question: What was 'JS fatigue'?
options: Mid-2010s phenomenon when the rapidly expanding JS tooling ecosystem felt overwhelming to learn
history-of-javascript.explanation: Babel, Webpack, ESLint, dozens of frameworks — it was hard to keep up. Today the community has consolidated around fewer mainstream tools.

history-of-javascript.question: What is TC39's role?
options: The committee at Ecma International that defines new ECMAScript features through stages 0-4
history-of-javascript.explanation: TC39 representatives from browser vendors and big tech meet regularly. Proposals advance through stages with specs, polyfills, and tests before becoming part of the language.

history-of-javascript.question: Why are annual ES releases significant?
options: Smaller, predictable yearly snapshots replaced waiting years for huge releases — easier to track and adopt
history-of-javascript.explanation: Post-ES6, the annual model lets features ship as soon as they're ready. Browsers can roll them out gradually instead of in massive 'big bang' updates.

history-of-javascript.question: What has driven JavaScript's enduring relevance?
options: Universal browser support, open governance, rich ecosystem, and constant evolution
history-of-javascript.explanation: JS is the lingua franca of the web. WebAssembly might run beside it, but JS remains the default API into the DOM and browser APIs.

javascript-versions.question: What does ES5 introduce that's still core today?
options: Strict mode, JSON support, Array methods (forEach/map/filter), and Object property descriptors
javascript-versions.explanation: ES5 (2009) was incremental but crucial: strict mode caught bugs, Array methods enabled functional patterns, and Object.defineProperty unlocked frameworks.

javascript-versions.question: Which feature came in ES6/ES2015?
options: let/const, arrow functions, classes, template literals, destructuring, modules, Promises
javascript-versions.explanation: ES6 modernized the language. Most modern JS code is ES6+ or transpiled to ES5 when targeting old browsers.

javascript-versions.question: Which version added async/await?
javascript-versions.explanation: async/await landed in ES2017, building on ES6 Promises. It made async code feel synchronous without callback hell or .then chains.

javascript-versions.question: Optional chaining (?.) shipped in?
javascript-versions.explanation: ES2020 added optional chaining and nullish coalescing (??). They simplified handling potentially undefined deep properties.

javascript-versions.question: What did ES2015 modules add?
options: import/export — a static module system replacing CJS in modern code
javascript-versions.explanation: ES Modules are statically analyzable, support tree-shaking, and now run natively in browsers and Node. Most ecosystems have moved or are moving to ESM.

javascript-versions.question: Which version introduced top-level await?
javascript-versions.explanation: ES2022 lets module-level code use await without an enclosing async function. Useful for module initialization that depends on async work.

javascript-versions.question: What's a 'living standard' in the context of JavaScript?
options: Annual ECMAScript snapshots plus continuous TC39 proposal pipeline — the language is always evolving
javascript-versions.explanation: Unlike many languages with major-version timelines, ECMAScript releases yearly while individual features advance through stages independently.

javascript-versions.question: How do older browsers run modern JS features?
options: Transpilers (Babel, SWC) compile modern syntax to older targets, plus polyfills for new APIs
javascript-versions.explanation: Combine Babel/SWC for syntax with core-js polyfills for new APIs. Browserslist specifies your target browsers; the toolchain produces compatible output.

javascript-versions.question: Why use 'use strict'?
options: Opt into stricter parsing/error rules — catches silent failures at runtime
javascript-versions.explanation: Strict mode disallows accidental globals, makes 'this' undefined in plain functions, and forbids syntax bound for future versions. Modules are strict by default.

javascript-versions.question: Which is a Stage 3 TC39 proposal example you should be aware of?
options: Decorators, Records & Tuples, Pipeline operator — proposals near acceptance you may see polyfilled
javascript-versions.explanation: Stage 3 proposals are likely to land. Tools like Babel let you experiment early, but be cautious — semantics can still change before Stage 4.

how-to-run-javascript.question: What's the simplest way to run JavaScript?
options: Open a browser DevTools console and execute it
how-to-run-javascript.explanation: Every modern browser ships a JS engine and a console. F12 → Console tab → type code, hit Enter — instant feedback, no install.

how-to-run-javascript.question: How do you load a JS file in HTML?
how-to-run-javascript.explanation: Use defer or type="module" to avoid blocking HTML parsing. Putting <script> at the end of <body> is a legacy alternative; defer is cleaner.

how-to-run-javascript.question: What's the difference between defer and async?
options: defer keeps document order and runs after parsing; async runs as soon as it loads, possibly out of order
how-to-run-javascript.explanation: Use defer for app code that must run in order. Use async for analytics-style scripts where order doesn't matter and you want them ASAP.

how-to-run-javascript.question: How do you run JavaScript from the command line?
options: Install Node.js (or Deno/Bun) and run `node script.js`
how-to-run-javascript.explanation: Node/Deno/Bun execute JS outside the browser. Bun and Deno also natively run TypeScript. They expose runtime APIs (FS, network, processes) browsers don't.

how-to-run-javascript.question: What's an HTML <script type="module">?
options: Loads the file as an ES Module — supports import/export and runs in strict mode by default
how-to-run-javascript.explanation: Modules are deferred by default, scoped (no global pollution), and use real import/export. Mixing module/non-module scripts is supported but non-trivial.

how-to-run-javascript.question: What's a REPL?
options: Read-Eval-Print Loop — interactive shell for one-line execution (node, deno, browser console)
how-to-run-javascript.explanation: Type code, see result. Great for quick experiments. Node ships one (just run `node`), as does Bun/Deno; browser DevTools is also a REPL.

how-to-run-javascript.question: How do online sandboxes (CodePen, JSFiddle, StackBlitz) run JS?
options: They run JS in your browser inside an iframe, often with a service worker proxy for module imports
how-to-run-javascript.explanation: StackBlitz can even run Node-style apps (Vite, Astro) entirely in the browser via WebContainers — no server execution at all.

how-to-run-javascript.question: What's nodemon?
options: A dev tool that restarts Node on file changes — improves the edit/run loop
how-to-run-javascript.explanation: Modern Node 18+ has --watch as a built-in flag, achieving similar functionality without nodemon. Bun's dev server also has hot reloading.

how-to-run-javascript.question: How do Vite/Webpack 'run' your JS during dev?
options: They serve a dev server, transform modules on demand or bundle, and provide HMR for fast updates
how-to-run-javascript.explanation: Vite leverages browser-native ESM and serves modules on the fly. Webpack bundles a single file. Both expose middleware for proxies and HMR.

how-to-run-javascript.question: Why use a sandbox/playground for quick JS experiments?
options: Zero setup, easy sharing, isolation from your machine, instant collaboration
how-to-run-javascript.explanation: CodePen/StackBlitz/Replit are great for demos, bug repros, and teaching. Easier than 'install Node, npm init, install deps, write file' for one-line experiments.

introduction-to-javascript.question: Which is a primitive value in JS?
introduction-to-javascript.explanation: Primitives: string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null, symbol. Everything else (objects, arrays, dates, functions) is a reference type.

introduction-to-javascript.question: Which statement is true about JavaScript?
options: Dynamically typed — variables aren't declared with a type and can hold any value
introduction-to-javascript.explanation: Types are checked at runtime. The same variable can hold a string, then a number, then an object — flexible but error-prone (TypeScript adds static checking).

introduction-to-javascript.question: How do you write a comment in JavaScript?
introduction-to-javascript.explanation: // for one-liners, /* ... */ for blocks (or doc comments /** ... */). HTML comments don't work in script bodies (legacy syntax notwithstanding).

introduction-to-javascript.question: What does console.log do?
options: Prints arguments to the runtime's console (browser DevTools or terminal)
introduction-to-javascript.explanation: Most-used debugging tool. Pass any number of args; objects render expandable in DevTools. Variants: console.error, console.warn, console.table.

introduction-to-javascript.question: How do you create a function?
introduction-to-javascript.explanation: Function declarations (hoisted), expressions, arrow functions, and methods inside objects/classes are all valid. Arrow functions are common for callbacks.

introduction-to-javascript.question: What's a variable in JavaScript?
options: A named reference to a value, declared with var/let/const
introduction-to-javascript.explanation: var has function scope (legacy). let/const have block scope. const can't be reassigned (but mutable contents — e.g., array push — still work).

introduction-to-javascript.question: What does '+' do with strings?
introduction-to-javascript.explanation: When either operand is a string, + concatenates. Mixing types coerces: '1' + 1 === '11'. Use template literals (`${x}-${y}`) for clarity.

introduction-to-javascript.question: Which loops over an object's enumerable string keys?
introduction-to-javascript.explanation: for...in iterates keys (including inherited ones — guard with hasOwnProperty). for...of iterates iterables (arrays, Maps, Sets, generators).

introduction-to-javascript.question: What's JSON in JavaScript?
options: JavaScript Object Notation — a text format for data, parsed/serialized via JSON.parse and JSON.stringify
introduction-to-javascript.explanation: JSON is a strict subset of JS object literal syntax — keys quoted, no comments, no functions, no undefined. Universal data interchange format.

introduction-to-javascript.question: Which is true about JavaScript objects?
options: Mutable key-value collections; values are accessed via dot or bracket notation
introduction-to-javascript.explanation: Objects are central to JS. Newer additions (Map, Set, WeakMap) handle special cases; plain objects remain the default.

all-about-variables.question: Which keyword should you prefer by default?
options: const, then let if reassignment is needed
all-about-variables.explanation: Default to const for clarity (no reassignment). Use let only when you need to reassign. var is legacy with confusing scoping rules.

all-about-variables.question: Which scoping model does var use?
all-about-variables.explanation: var ignores {} blocks. A var declared inside an if {} is visible throughout the enclosing function. let/const are block-scoped.

all-about-variables.question: What's the temporal dead zone (TDZ)?
options: The window between entering a let/const's scope and the line where it's declared, where access throws ReferenceError
all-about-variables.explanation: let/const are hoisted but uninitialized until their declaration. Accessing them in the TDZ throws — preventing the silent-undefined bug var has.

all-about-variables.question: Can you redeclare a const?
options: No — duplicate declaration is a syntax error
all-about-variables.explanation: Both let and const cannot be redeclared in the same scope. var allows it (yet another reason it's discouraged).

all-about-variables.question: Does const make the value immutable?
options: No — const prevents reassignment of the binding; the value (e.g., array contents) can still mutate
all-about-variables.explanation: const arr = [1,2]; arr.push(3) is allowed — only `arr = [...]` reassignment is forbidden. Use Object.freeze for shallow immutability.

all-about-variables.question: What's a global variable in browser JS?
options: A property of the window object — e.g., undeclared assignments or var at top level
all-about-variables.explanation: Avoid creating globals — they pollute the namespace. Modules (script type="module") have their own scope, eliminating accidental globals.

all-about-variables.question: What's variable shadowing?
options: An inner scope declaring a same-named variable, hiding the outer one within that scope
all-about-variables.explanation: Shadowing is legal but can be confusing. Modern linters warn on it. Pick distinct names or use destructuring with renaming when conflicts arise.

all-about-variables.question: What does 'use strict' do for variables?
options: Forbids using a variable without declaration (no implicit globals)
all-about-variables.explanation: Without strict mode, `x = 1` (no var/let/const) silently creates a global. Strict mode throws ReferenceError — catching typos early. Modules are strict by default.

all-about-variables.question: What's destructuring assignment?
options: Pattern syntax to extract values from arrays/objects into variables: const {a, b} = obj
all-about-variables.explanation: Destructuring tightens code. Defaults, renames, and rest are all supported: const {x: localX = 0, ...rest} = obj — clean and expressive.

all-about-variables.question: What's the rest pattern in variable assignment?
options: ...name collects remaining elements into a new array/object: const [first, ...rest] = arr
all-about-variables.explanation: Useful for splitting head/tail or extracting known props while keeping the rest: const {a, ...others} = props. Spread (...) is the inverse for expanding.

var.question: What's var's scoping?
var.explanation: A var inside an if/for ignores those blocks — it's hoisted to the enclosing function (or globally if outside any function).

var.question: What value does a var have before its declaration line is reached?
options: undefined (declaration is hoisted; initialization is not)
var.explanation: var declarations get hoisted with an undefined initializer. Reading them before assignment yields undefined — silent and bug-prone.

var.question: Why is var generally avoided in modern code?
options: Function scoping causes leaks; hoisting causes silent undefined; let/const are clearer
var.explanation: let/const fix var's footguns: block scope, no silent undefined, no redeclaration. Most code style guides ban var.

var.question: Can var be redeclared?
options: Yes — multiple var declarations of the same name in the same scope are allowed
var.explanation: var x = 1; var x = 2; — legal. let/const throw at the second declaration. Linters typically forbid var redeclarations regardless.

var.question: What does `for(var i=0; ...) { setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0); }` log?
options: The final value of i (after the loop) repeated — classic var-in-closure pitfall
var.explanation: var creates a single i shared across all closures. By the time setTimeout fires, the loop has finished. let creates a fresh binding per iteration.

var.question: Where does var attached to globalThis?
options: Top-level var in a classic script becomes a property of globalThis (window in browsers)
var.explanation: ES Modules (and let/const) don't pollute globalThis. Classic-script var does — making accidental name collisions easy in legacy projects.

var.question: What's the difference between var and let in a block?
options: let is block-scoped; var leaks to the enclosing function
var.explanation: if (true) { let a; var b; } — outside the if, a is undefined (gone), b is accessible (leaked).

var.question: Does var support the temporal dead zone?
var.explanation: TDZ is a let/const feature. Reading a var before its declaration line returns undefined, not a ReferenceError.

var.question: Is var useful anywhere in modern code?
options: Rarely — almost always replaced by let/const
var.explanation: Some legacy codebases keep var for consistency. New code overwhelmingly uses let/const. Many lint configs ban var entirely.

var.question: What does function-level var hoisting mean for a parameter named the same?
options: var redeclaration of a parameter is silently ignored (parameter retains its value)
var.explanation: function f(x){ var x = 5; } — x is the parameter, then reassigned to 5. var doesn't double-declare; it's effectively the assignment.

let.question: What's let's scoping?
let.explanation: let is the modern way to declare reassignable variables. Each {} block (if, for, function body, etc.) limits its visibility.

let.question: Can you redeclare let in the same scope?
let.explanation: let prevents accidental shadowing within the same scope. Redeclare in a nested block is fine (that's a new scope).

let.question: What happens with `for (let i=0; ...)` and closures?
options: Each iteration gets its own i binding — closures see distinct values
let.explanation: let-in-for creates a fresh binding per iteration. setTimeout callbacks correctly log 0,1,2,... — fixing the classic var pitfall.

let.question: Is let hoisted?
options: Yes, but unreachable in the TDZ until the declaration line
let.explanation: Hoisted means the declaration is allocated when the scope starts, but reading before initialization throws ReferenceError (TDZ).

let.question: When should you use let over const?
options: When the binding genuinely needs to be reassigned (counters, accumulators)
let.explanation: Default to const. Use let when you must reassign (let count = 0; count++). Many style guides require const-by-default with linter rules.

let.question: What's wrong with `let x = 1; let x = 2;` at the top of a script?
let.explanation: Same scope can have only one let with a given name. This catches typos that var would silently allow.

let.question: Does let pollute globalThis at the top level?
options: No — top-level let/const are not properties of window/globalThis
let.explanation: let/const at script top level go in a separate 'global lexical environment'. var does become a globalThis property — another reason to prefer let/const.

let.question: When is let preferred over var even in older codebases?
options: Always — let is strictly safer (block scope, no silent undefined, no redeclaration)
let.explanation: Modernize var → let or const when refactoring. Behavior is more predictable, eslint can enforce, and bugs around scoping disappear.

let.question: What does `if (true) { let a = 1 }` do outside the if?
options: ReferenceError on access (a doesn't exist outside)
let.explanation: Block-scoped means a only exists inside the {}. Outside, accessing a is a ReferenceError because no such binding exists.

let.question: Can let be used at the top of a module?
options: Yes — it's just block scope where the module is the outermost block
let.explanation: Modules have their own top-level scope (not global). let/const there are visible throughout the module but not outside it.

const.question: What does const guarantee?
options: The binding can't be reassigned (but the referenced object can still mutate)
const.explanation: const arr = [1]; arr.push(2) — works. arr = [3] — TypeError. Use Object.freeze for shallow read-only objects.

const.question: Must const be initialized at declaration?
const.explanation: Because const can't be reassigned, leaving it uninitialized would make it permanently undefined — the spec disallows this.

const.question: What's const's scoping?
const.explanation: Identical to let. Both follow block-scope rules and live in the temporal dead zone until their declaration.

const.question: Can you mutate an object declared with const?
options: Yes — properties can change; only reassignment of the binding is forbidden
const.explanation: const user = {name: 'a'}; user.name = 'b' — fine. user = {} — TypeError. The 'const' applies to the variable, not the contents.

const.question: Why prefer const by default?
options: Communicates intent (won't change), prevents accidental reassignment, easier to reason about
const.explanation: Code reviewers can trust the variable points to the same value throughout its scope. Many style guides enforce const-by-default via eslint's prefer-const rule.

const.question: What if you need a deeply immutable object?
options: Use Object.freeze (shallow) or libraries like immer/Immutable.js for deep immutability
const.explanation: Object.freeze freezes one level. For deep immutability, recursively freeze (deepFreeze) or use a library. TypeScript's `as const` adds compile-time read-only typing.

const.question: Is const hoisted?
const.explanation: Same hoisting + TDZ semantics as let. Accessing before declaration throws ReferenceError.

const.question: Can you use const for loop variables?
options: Yes for `for...of`/`for...in` (each iteration has its own const), but not for traditional `for(;;)` with reassignment
const.explanation: for (const x of arr) — works. for (const i = 0; i < 10; i++) — fails because i++ mutates. Use let for traditional counters.

const.question: What's `as const` in TypeScript?
options: A type assertion that makes literal values readonly and narrows their types
const.explanation: const tup = [1, 2] as const; — type is readonly [1, 2] instead of number[]. Useful for tuples and discriminated unions.

const.question: Does const prevent property addition on a non-frozen object?
options: No — only the binding is constant; properties can be added/changed/deleted
const.explanation: const config = {}; config.url = 'x' — works. To prevent additions, use Object.freeze, Object.seal, or a typed read-only declaration.

variable-declarations.question: What's the modern recommended order of preference?
variable-declarations.explanation: Default to const. Use let only when reassignment is needed. Avoid var unless maintaining legacy code that requires it.

variable-declarations.question: Which declaration causes the temporal dead zone?
variable-declarations.explanation: var hoists with undefined (no TDZ). let/const are hoisted but unreachable until their declaration line — accessing them earlier throws.

variable-declarations.question: What's a destructuring declaration?
options: A variable declaration that pulls values from an iterable/object: const {a, b} = obj
variable-declarations.explanation: Destructuring works with let/const/var. It supports defaults, renaming, and rest: const {x: lx = 0, ...rest} = obj.

variable-declarations.question: What's the difference between `let a, b;` and `let a; let b;`?
options: Functionally identical — comma-list is just shorthand
variable-declarations.explanation: let supports a comma-separated list of declarations in one statement, just like var. Each variable is independently hoisted/initialized.

variable-declarations.question: Can you mix declarations like `const a = 1, b;`?
options: No — const requires every declaration in the list to have an initializer
variable-declarations.explanation: All const declarations must initialize. The error happens at parse time. Use let for the uninitialized one or initialize b too.

variable-declarations.question: What does `function f(x = 0) {}` do for x?
options: Default parameter — x = 0 if argument is undefined
variable-declarations.explanation: Default parameters apply when the argument is undefined (explicit pass of undefined still triggers the default). null does not — it's an explicit 'no value'.

variable-declarations.question: What's a global declaration in modules vs classic scripts?
options: Classic scripts: top-level var becomes globalThis property. Modules: nothing leaks to globalThis
variable-declarations.explanation: ES Modules introduced clean module scoping. Migrating from script tags to type="module" eliminates accidental global leaks at the top level.

variable-declarations.question: Does declaring without var/let/const work in strict mode?
options: No — assigning to an undeclared variable throws ReferenceError
variable-declarations.explanation: x = 5 with no declaration is allowed in sloppy mode (creates a global) but throws in strict mode. Modules are strict by default.

variable-declarations.question: What's the spread/rest pattern interaction with declarations?
options: Used to expand or collect: const [a, ...rest] = arr; const {x, ...others} = obj
variable-declarations.explanation: Spread (...) expands; rest (...) collects. Same syntax, role determined by context. Powerful with const declarations for clean immutability patterns.

variable-declarations.question: Is `let undefined = 5;` allowed?
options: No in strict mode (undefined is a non-writable identifier in strict mode)
variable-declarations.explanation: ES5+ made undefined a non-writable property of the global object. In strict mode, you can't redeclare it. In sloppy mode it's allowed locally but generally a terrible idea.

hoisting.question: What is hoisting?
options: JavaScript's behavior of moving declarations to the top of their scope before code execution
hoisting.explanation: Function and var declarations are 'hoisted' to the top of their scope. Initializations stay in place. let/const are hoisted but stay in the TDZ until declared.

hoisting.question: What does `console.log(x); var x = 5;` log?
hoisting.explanation: var x is hoisted; the assignment isn't. So x exists as undefined when console.log runs. let/const would throw a ReferenceError instead (TDZ).

hoisting.question: Are function declarations hoisted?
options: Yes — entire definition is hoisted, callable before its line
hoisting.explanation: function foo(){} can be called from above the declaration. Function expressions (`const foo = function(){}`) follow var/let/const rules and aren't fully hoisted.

hoisting.question: Are class declarations hoisted?
options: Hoisted, but in TDZ — can't be used before declaration
hoisting.explanation: Classes behave like let — the binding exists at scope start but is unusable until the declaration line is reached.

hoisting.question: What does `console.log(x); let x = 5;` do?
options: ReferenceError because x is in the TDZ
hoisting.explanation: let is hoisted but accessing it before initialization throws — preventing the silent undefined that var allows.

hoisting.question: What's a mental model for hoisting?
options: Declarations are 'discovered' at scope entry; assignments execute in order
hoisting.explanation: Hoisting isn't physical movement; the engine just processes the scope twice — first finding declarations, then executing line by line.

hoisting.question: Can you call a function expression before it's defined?
options: No — function expressions follow var/let/const rules; only their binding is hoisted
hoisting.explanation: var foo = function(){}; — calling foo() above the declaration sees undefined and throws TypeError. Function declarations are special-cased.

hoisting.question: What's the order between var hoisting and function hoisting in the same scope?
options: Function declarations are hoisted first; var declarations don't override them
hoisting.explanation: If both share a name, the function declaration wins at hoist time. Subsequent var-assignments execute in order and may overwrite the function.

hoisting.question: Why is hoisting historically problematic?
options: Silent undefined values, surprising code-order independence — let/const + linters fix this in modern code
hoisting.explanation: Pre-ES6 code often had bugs where var was used before it appeared declared. Modern style strongly prefers declaring before use, plus let/const's TDZ.

hoisting.question: Is `typeof x` for an undeclared x an error?
options: No (in non-TDZ) — it returns 'undefined' (special exception). With let/const in TDZ it throws
hoisting.explanation: typeof on a never-declared identifier is the only safe access pattern (returns 'undefined'). But on a let/const in its TDZ, even typeof throws.

variable-naming-rules.question: Which is a valid identifier in JS?
variable-naming-rules.explanation: Identifiers must start with a letter, $, or _. Then letters, digits, $, _. Hyphens and spaces are not allowed.

variable-naming-rules.question: What's a reserved word example?
variable-naming-rules.explanation: JS reserves syntax keywords (if, while, class, return, typeof, ...). They can't be used as identifiers. await/yield are reserved in some contexts.

variable-naming-rules.question: What's the standard naming convention for variables in JS?
options: camelCase for variables/functions, PascalCase for classes/components, UPPER_SNAKE for constants
variable-naming-rules.explanation: myVariable, MyClass, MAX_RETRIES — the JS community has settled on these conventions, enforced by linters in many style guides.

variable-naming-rules.question: Can identifiers contain Unicode?
options: Yes — identifiers can include Unicode letters (e.g., café), but most code stays in ASCII
variable-naming-rules.explanation: ECMAScript supports Unicode in identifiers. Practical advice: stick to ASCII for portability and tool support.

variable-naming-rules.question: Is JavaScript case-sensitive?
options: Yes — userName and username are different identifiers
variable-naming-rules.explanation: All identifiers are case-sensitive. This is a common source of bugs when typos vary in case.

variable-naming-rules.question: What's a magic number?
options: A literal value with no obvious meaning — extract it into a named constant for clarity
variable-naming-rules.explanation: if (status === 3) is unclear. const STATUS_APPROVED = 3; if (status === STATUS_APPROVED) reads better and centralizes the meaning.

variable-naming-rules.question: Why prefix private fields with _ historically?
options: Convention to signal 'internal'; modern JS has actual private fields with #
variable-naming-rules.explanation: Pre-ES2022, _ was just a hint — anyone could still access. Now `class { #secret = 1 }` enforces true privacy at the language level.

variable-naming-rules.question: What's the convention for boolean variables?
options: Prefix with is/has/can/should — isReady, hasErrors, canEdit
variable-naming-rules.explanation: Boolean prefixes make intent clear at the call site (if (isReady)). Linters can warn on plain boolean names like `ready`.

variable-naming-rules.question: What's a sensible function naming pattern?
options: verbNoun (getUser, fetchPosts, calculateTotal) — describes the action
variable-naming-rules.explanation: Verb-led names communicate behavior. Pure-data accessors might use just nouns (currentUser as a getter).

variable-naming-rules.question: Is naming critical for code quality?
options: Yes — clear names are one of the highest-leverage things you can do for maintainability
variable-naming-rules.explanation: Names appear everywhere. Good ones eliminate the need for comments. 'There are only two hard things in CS: cache invalidation and naming things.'

variable-scopes.question: What's lexical (static) scope?
options: A scope determined by where code is written, not where it runs from — the rule JS follows
variable-scopes.explanation: JS uses lexical scoping. A function's scope chain is fixed by its definition, not by who called it. Closures rely on this.

variable-scopes.question: What scopes does JavaScript have?
options: Global, module, function, block (let/const), and lexical environments closed over by functions
variable-scopes.explanation: Each function call creates a new scope. let/const create per-block scopes. Modules have their own top-level scope.

variable-scopes.question: What's the global scope?
options: The outermost scope — globalThis (window in browsers, global in Node) for classic scripts; modules have a separate module-level scope
variable-scopes.explanation: Polluting the global scope risks collisions. ES Modules avoid implicit global pollution; declarations stay in the module scope.

variable-scopes.question: What's a closure?
options: A function that retains access to variables in its outer lexical scope after the outer function returns
variable-scopes.explanation: Closures are JS's primary mechanism for data privacy and stateful callbacks. They're created automatically every time a function is created.

variable-scopes.question: What's IIFE used for?
options: Immediately Invoked Function Expression — creates a private scope, common pre-ES6 to avoid globals
variable-scopes.explanation: (function(){ ...code... })() runs immediately and any var declarations are scoped inside. With ES Modules + block scope, IIFE is largely unnecessary.

variable-scopes.question: How do block scopes interact with for-loops and let?
options: Each iteration of `for (let i...)` creates a new i binding — closures capture distinct values
variable-scopes.explanation: This per-iteration binding is the fix for the infamous var-in-setTimeout closure problem. Each iteration's i is independent.

variable-scopes.question: What is the scope chain?
options: When resolving an identifier, JS walks outward from the current scope through enclosing scopes until found (or reports an error)
variable-scopes.explanation: Inner scopes can read outer scope's variables (via closure). Outer scopes can't read inner. The chain ends at globalThis.

variable-scopes.question: Can a block create a scope without a function?
options: Yes — { let x = 1 } creates a scope; outside, x is gone
variable-scopes.explanation: Standalone blocks are valid. Combined with let/const, they create localized scopes useful for limiting variable lifetime in long functions.

variable-scopes.question: What's a closure pitfall in async code?
options: Capturing variables that change after the closure is created — leading to surprising values when callbacks run
variable-scopes.explanation: Classic example: var i in a loop with setTimeout. Modern fixes: use let, copy by value, or bind/wrap in an IIFE.

variable-scopes.question: Why does the 'module pattern' use closures?
options: To create private state — variables inside the IIFE are inaccessible from outside, exposed only via returned API
variable-scopes.explanation: Pre-class fields, the module pattern (IIFE returning an object) gave you private internal state. Modern alternatives: classes with #private, or modules with non-exported variables.

data-types.question: How many primitive types does JS have?
options: 7 (string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null, symbol)
data-types.explanation: Everything else (objects, arrays, functions, dates) is a reference type — they're all 'object' under the hood.

data-types.question: What's the value type of `typeof null`?
data-types.explanation: Preserved for backwards compatibility. Use `value === null` to test for null specifically. typeof undefined correctly returns 'undefined'.

data-types.question: What's the difference between `undefined` and `null`?
options: undefined: variable hasn't been assigned. null: explicit 'no value' assigned by code
data-types.explanation: Convention: undefined = absence of assignment (function returns nothing). null = intentional emptiness. They're not equal with === but are with ==.

data-types.question: What's a Symbol used for?
options: Unique identifier, often as object property keys that won't collide
data-types.explanation: Symbol() always produces a unique value. Useful for non-enumerable property keys, well-known protocols (Symbol.iterator).

data-types.question: How do you check if a value is an array?
data-types.explanation: typeof returns 'object' for arrays. Array.isArray is the reliable way; works across realms (iframes) where instanceof can fail.

data-types.question: What does NaN stand for?
options: Not a Number — produced by failed numeric operations (e.g., 'foo' / 2)
data-types.explanation: NaN is a special number value. Bizarrely, NaN !== NaN. Test with Number.isNaN(value) — never with == NaN.

data-types.question: Why is BigInt useful?
options: Represent integers beyond Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (2^53 - 1) without precision loss
data-types.explanation: BigInt (literal: 1n, or BigInt('123')) handles huge integers exactly. Can't mix with Number arithmetic without conversion.

data-types.question: Are JavaScript strings mutable?
options: No — strings are immutable; methods like .toUpperCase() return new strings
data-types.explanation: Reassigning a variable doesn't mutate the original string. This makes strings safe to share across scopes without unexpected changes.

data-types.question: What's the difference between primitive and reference types?
options: Primitives copy by value; references copy the reference (multiple variables see the same object)
data-types.explanation: let a = {}; let b = a; b.x = 1; — a.x is also 1. For primitives, b is a separate copy. Understanding this avoids many bugs.

data-types.question: What does `typeof function(){}` return?
options: 'function' (special-cased; functions are technically a callable object)
data-types.explanation: typeof returns 'function' for callable values (functions, classes). That makes feature-detecting callable values straightforward.

string.question: How do you create a multi-line string?
options: Use a template literal with backticks: `line1\nline2`
string.explanation: Template literals (backticks) preserve actual newlines. \n works inside any string. Concatenation works but is verbose.

string.question: What does template literal interpolation look like?
string.explanation: `Hello, ${name}!` embeds expressions. Fits common patterns (URLs, messages) much better than concatenation.

string.question: Are JavaScript strings mutable?
string.explanation: Strings are primitives; methods like .toUpperCase(), .replace(), .slice() always return new strings. Reassign to keep results.

string.question: Which method extracts part of a string?
string.explanation: slice is the modern recommended method (supports negative indices). substr is deprecated. substring exists for legacy reasons.

string.question: What does .split(',') return?
options: An array of substrings split by the separator
string.explanation: 'a,b,c'.split(',') → ['a', 'b', 'c']. Pass a limit to cap the result; pass a regex for complex separators.

string.question: How do you check if a string contains a substring?
string.explanation: .includes('foo') returns true/false. .indexOf returns the position (or -1). startsWith/endsWith also exist for specific positions.

string.question: What's the difference between == and === for strings?
options: === requires both sides be strings; == will coerce
string.explanation: Always prefer ===. == coerces ('5' == 5 is true), which causes confusing bugs. Use === for predictable behavior.

string.question: What does .padStart(4, '0') do?
options: Pads the string at the start with '0' to reach length 4
string.explanation: '7'.padStart(4, '0') → '0007'. Useful for formatting numbers/dates. .padEnd works at the end.

string.question: How do you remove whitespace from string ends?
string.explanation: .trim() removes leading and trailing whitespace. Helpful for processing user input from forms.

string.question: What does .replaceAll vs .replace do?
options: replace replaces only the first occurrence (with a string); replaceAll replaces all
string.explanation: Pre-replaceAll (ES2021), people used .replace(/foo/g, 'bar'). replaceAll with a plain string makes intent clearer and avoids regex escaping.

number.question: What numeric type does JS have for non-bigint numbers?
number.explanation: Surprises follow: 0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3 (binary floating point). Use libraries (decimal.js) for exact decimal math (currency).

number.question: What is Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER?
options: 2^53 - 1 (9007199254740991) — the largest integer that can be represented exactly as a Number
number.explanation: Beyond MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, precision degrades. For larger integers, use BigInt. Be careful with IDs from APIs that exceed this range.

number.question: What does parseInt('10', 2) return?
number.explanation: parseInt's second argument is the radix. Always pass it explicitly to avoid surprises (octal interpretation in old code).

number.question: How do you check if a value is NaN?
number.explanation: NaN !== NaN, so equality fails. Number.isNaN strictly checks for NaN. The global isNaN coerces first ('foo' becomes NaN), so it's less precise.

number.question: What does 0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3 evaluate to?
number.explanation: Classic floating-point gotcha. Compare with a small epsilon: Math.abs(a - b) < Number.EPSILON for fuzzy equality.

number.question: What's the difference between Math.floor, Math.ceil, Math.round?
options: floor → toward -∞; ceil → toward +∞; round → to nearest (.5 → up)
number.explanation: Math.trunc truncates toward 0. JS's round breaks .5 ties upward (Math.round(2.5) === 3, Math.round(-2.5) === -2). Watch for edge cases.

number.question: Why might (0.1).toFixed(2) be useful?
options: Format a number to N decimal places as a string — useful for display
number.explanation: Returns a string. Don't use for further math (rounding errors). Intl.NumberFormat is better for localized currency/percent formatting.

number.question: What's Number.EPSILON?
options: The smallest difference between 1 and the next representable number — useful for fuzzy float comparisons
number.explanation: About 2.2e-16. Practical fuzzy equality: Math.abs(a - b) < Number.EPSILON. For larger magnitudes, scale epsilon by max(|a|,|b|).

number.question: Which converts a string to a number?
number.explanation: Number('10') === 10. +'10' is a quick coercion. parseInt allows radix and stops at non-digits. Number is strict (returns NaN for partial matches).

number.question: What does Number.isInteger(1.0) return?
number.explanation: JS has no separate integer type. Number.isInteger checks if the value has no fractional part. 1.0 and 1 are the same Number.

boolean.question: Which values are falsy in JavaScript?
boolean.explanation: Memorize the 7 falsy values. Everything else (including '0', 'false', [], {}) is truthy. Be careful: empty arrays/objects are TRUTHY.

boolean.question: What does !!value do?
options: Converts value to its boolean equivalent (truthy → true, falsy → false)
boolean.explanation: Two NOT operators coerce to boolean. Equivalent to Boolean(value). Useful when an API expects a strict boolean.

boolean.question: What does the || operator do?
options: Logical OR — returns the first truthy operand (or the last if all falsy)
boolean.explanation: name = input || 'default' — uses 'default' if input is falsy. Note: '' or 0 trigger the default. Use ?? if only null/undefined should.

boolean.question: What does ?? (nullish coalescing) do differently from ||?
options: ?? falls back only for null/undefined (not 0, '', false)
boolean.explanation: value ?? 'default' — keeps 0 or '' as valid values, replacing only null/undefined. Often what you actually want for default values.

boolean.question: What's the result of `'' && 'b'`?
boolean.explanation: && returns the first falsy operand or the last if all truthy. So `0 && x` → 0, `1 && 2` → 2.

boolean.question: What does `!arr.length` evaluate to for arr = []?
boolean.explanation: [].length === 0; !0 === true. Common pattern to check empty arrays. For empty objects, Object.keys(obj).length is the equivalent.

boolean.question: What's a 'truthiness check'?
options: if (value) ... — passes for any truthy value, fails only for the 7 falsy ones
boolean.explanation: Convenient but be careful: if (count) — fails when count is 0 (intended valid value). Then check count !== 0 explicitly.

boolean.question: What does Boolean(value) do?
options: Returns true if value is truthy, false otherwise — explicit coercion
boolean.explanation: Same as !!value. Boolean is explicit and self-documenting; some prefer it for readability over !!.

boolean.question: Why prefer === over == for booleans?
options: == coerces (1 == true is true; '' == 0 is true) — leads to bugs. === checks type and value
boolean.explanation: Loose equality has many surprising rules. === eliminates them — strongly recommended in modern style guides.

boolean.question: What's the result of `!!{}` and `!![]`?
options: Both true (empty object and array are truthy)
boolean.explanation: Despite seeming 'empty', objects and arrays are reference types — always truthy. Common interview gotcha.

undefined.question: When is a variable undefined?
options: When declared but not assigned, when accessing missing object props, when a function returns nothing, when a parameter is omitted
undefined.explanation: undefined is JS's default 'no value' state. Convention: don't assign undefined manually — use null for explicit emptiness.

undefined.question: What does typeof undefined return?
undefined.explanation: Unlike null (which returns 'object' due to a historical bug), undefined correctly returns 'undefined'.

undefined.question: How do you check for undefined safely?
undefined.explanation: === is direct. typeof works even for never-declared identifiers (no ReferenceError). Both are correct; typeof is for paranoid checks.

undefined.question: Is undefined a keyword?
options: No — it's a global property (in strict mode it's read-only)
undefined.explanation: Pre-ES5, you could shadow undefined locally and break things. ES5 made it non-writable on the global object. Modules are strict by default.

undefined.question: What does a function return if it has no return statement?
undefined.explanation: Functions without explicit return (or `return;`) implicitly return undefined. Same for void operator usage.

undefined.question: What happens with default parameters when undefined is passed?
options: Default kicks in (undefined triggers default; null does not)
undefined.explanation: function f(x = 5) {} — f() → 5. f(undefined) → 5. f(null) → null. The default activates only on undefined.

undefined.question: What does `delete obj.x` do?
options: Removes the property; subsequent access yields undefined
undefined.explanation: delete is rarely necessary in modern code. To remove a key, prefer immutable patterns: `const {x, ...rest} = obj`.

undefined.question: Is `undefined === undefined` true?
undefined.explanation: Unlike NaN, undefined equals itself. This makes the === undefined check reliable.

undefined.question: What's an idiomatic way to set defaults from possibly-undefined values?
undefined.explanation: ?? is the modern default. || would also fall back for '' or 0 — typically not desired.

undefined.question: Why does optional chaining (?.) help with undefined?
options: Returns undefined instead of throwing when an intermediate value is null/undefined: a?.b?.c
undefined.explanation: Saves writing if (a && a.b && a.b.c). Combine with ?? for default: a?.b?.c ?? 'fallback'.

null.question: What's the type of null?
options: typeof returns 'object' (historical bug); semantically it's a primitive
null.explanation: Use `value === null` to test for null. typeof can't reliably distinguish null from object.

null.question: When should you use null?
options: When you intentionally want to indicate 'no value' or 'empty' — distinct from 'not yet assigned' (undefined)
null.explanation: Convention: null is explicit, undefined is implicit. APIs returning JSON typically use null for missing fields (JSON has no undefined).

null.question: Is null === undefined?
null.explanation: Strictly different. With ==, null == undefined is true (loose equality treats them equivalent). === gives the safer answer.

null.question: What does Number(null) return?
null.explanation: Number(null) coerces to 0. Number(undefined) returns NaN. Subtle inconsistency that catches newcomers.

null.question: What's a 'null check'?
options: Guarding code against null/undefined before using a value: if (user) ...
null.explanation: Optional chaining and nullish coalescing made null checks more concise. TypeScript's strictNullChecks catches missing checks at compile time.

null.question: Which is safer: `if (value)` or `if (value != null)`?
options: if (value != null) when you only want to skip null/undefined (allows 0, '', false)
null.explanation: value != null is true for everything except null and undefined. if (value) also fails for 0, '', false — usually unintended.

null.question: What's `typeof null`?
null.explanation: Spec authors agreed it's a bug but breaking the web isn't worth fixing it. Just use === null for null tests.

null.question: What does JSON.stringify(null) produce?
null.explanation: JSON has null but no undefined. Properties with undefined values are dropped during stringify; null is preserved.

null.question: What is null prototype useful for?
options: Object.create(null) creates an object without inherited properties — safer as a hash map
null.explanation: Default {} inherits from Object.prototype (toString, hasOwnProperty). Object.create(null) avoids these — useful when keys come from user input that could collide with built-ins.

null.question: What does `null + 1` evaluate to?
null.explanation: + coerces null to 0. Many such coercions are surprising — TypeScript or strict checks can catch unintended ones.

bigint.question: How do you create a BigInt?
options: Suffix integer literal with n: 123n; or BigInt(123)
bigint.explanation: 123n and BigInt('123') (or BigInt(123)) both work. Mixing BigInt with Number in arithmetic throws TypeError.

bigint.question: What's the main use case for BigInt?
options: Integers larger than Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (2^53 - 1) without precision loss
bigint.explanation: Database IDs, cryptography, or precise large-integer math benefit from BigInt. Currency is better handled with decimal libraries (BigInt is integers only).

bigint.question: Can you mix BigInt and Number directly?
options: No — TypeError. Convert explicitly: BigInt(num) or Number(big)
bigint.explanation: Mixing is intentionally disallowed because precision could silently degrade. Force a choice with explicit conversion.

bigint.question: What's typeof 10n?
bigint.explanation: BigInt has its own type tag. Use typeof for type checks; cast carefully when storing or serializing.

bigint.question: Can BigInt be JSON-serialized?
options: No — JSON.stringify throws TypeError on BigInt; you need to convert to string first
bigint.explanation: Use a replacer or convert BigInts to strings: JSON.stringify(obj, (_,v) => typeof v === 'bigint' ? v.toString() : v).

bigint.question: What's the result of 10n / 3n?
bigint.explanation: BigInt arithmetic is integer-only. Use BigInt for exact-integer math; for fractions use Number or a decimal library.

bigint.question: Is BigInt always slower than Number?
options: Often slower due to arbitrary precision; engines optimize but use BigInt only when needed
bigint.explanation: BigInt operations grow with the number of digits. Use Number when precision allows; BigInt when precision matters.

bigint.question: What's a common use case for BigInt in web development?
options: Working with 64-bit IDs from APIs (e.g., Twitter snowflake IDs) without losing precision
bigint.explanation: Some APIs return numeric IDs > 2^53. Without BigInt, those round to incorrect values silently. Treat them as strings or BigInts.

bigint.question: Can you use < > comparisons between BigInt and Number?
options: Yes — comparisons work; equality is per-value (1n == 1 is true loosely; === is false)
bigint.explanation: Order comparisons coerce safely. Strict equality requires same type. Use === Number(...) for stricter comparisons in practice.

bigint.question: What error type does mixing Number + BigInt throw?
bigint.explanation: Designed to be loud — silent precision loss is more dangerous than a thrown error. Always convert explicitly.

symbol.question: How do you create a Symbol?
symbol.explanation: Symbol() (with optional description) returns a unique primitive. `new Symbol()` throws — Symbols aren't constructed with `new`.

symbol.question: Are two Symbols with the same description equal?
options: No — every Symbol() call returns a unique value, even with the same description
symbol.explanation: The description is for debugging only. Symbol('id') !== Symbol('id'). Use Symbol.for(key) for cross-realm shared symbols by key.

symbol.question: What's a primary use case for Symbols?
options: Object property keys that won't accidentally collide with string keys (e.g., metadata, hidden methods)
symbol.explanation: Library authors use Symbols for internal API extensions on user objects without polluting their visible keys.

symbol.question: What's Symbol.iterator used for?
options: A well-known symbol that lets an object be iterated by for...of and spread
symbol.explanation: Implement [Symbol.iterator]() returning an object with next() to make any object iterable. Generators do this automatically.

symbol.question: Are symbol-keyed properties enumerable in for...in?
options: No — symbol keys are skipped by for...in/Object.keys; use Object.getOwnPropertySymbols
symbol.explanation: This invisibility is a feature: utility code (Object.keys, JSON.stringify) won't trip over your symbol-keyed metadata.

symbol.question: What does Symbol.for('id') do?
options: Returns a globally registered Symbol — identical across calls/realms with the same key
symbol.explanation: Useful when you need a Symbol shared between modules or iframes/workers — it's looked up in a global registry by key.

symbol.question: Can Symbols be coerced to strings?
options: Implicit coercion (e.g., '' + Symbol()) throws TypeError; explicit String(Symbol()) works
symbol.explanation: The throw on implicit conversion catches accidental concatenation. Use .description, .toString(), or String() for explicit conversion.

symbol.question: Are Symbols included in JSON.stringify?
options: No — symbol keys and values are silently skipped
symbol.explanation: JSON has no Symbol concept. If you must persist Symbol-keyed data, convert to string keys or use a custom replacer/serializer.

symbol.question: What are well-known Symbols?
options: Spec-defined Symbols (Symbol.iterator, Symbol.asyncIterator, Symbol.toPrimitive, Symbol.hasInstance, ...) that customize built-in behavior
symbol.explanation: Implementing these Symbol-keyed methods lets you make objects iterable, customize coercion, or change instanceof behavior.

symbol.question: Why use Symbols for 'private' fields?
options: Symbol-keyed properties aren't visible in standard property iteration — historical 'private' pattern. Modern alternative: # private fields in classes
symbol.explanation: Symbol-based privacy is convention. ES2022's #private is enforced by the language. Prefer # for new code; Symbols for cross-class extension.

object.question: How do you create an empty object?
object.explanation: Object literals are concise and idiomatic. Use Object.create(null) for a prototype-less hash-map use case.

object.question: How to access a property dynamically?
object.explanation: Dot notation requires a literal name. Brackets evaluate any expression: obj[key], obj['my key'], obj[Symbol(...)].

object.question: What does Object.keys(obj) return?
options: An array of own, enumerable, string-keyed property names
object.explanation: Skips inherited and symbol-keyed properties. Use Reflect.ownKeys for everything own (strings + symbols). For-in includes inherited string keys.

object.question: How do you copy an object shallowly?
object.explanation: Spread/assign do shallow copies. Nested objects are still shared by reference. JSON round-trip is a deep clone but loses functions, undefined, dates.

object.question: What does Object.freeze do?
options: Makes the object's own properties non-writable and non-configurable (shallow freeze)
object.explanation: Nested objects aren't frozen. For deep immutability, recurse. Object.isFrozen tests state.

object.question: How do you check if a property exists own (not inherited)?
object.explanation: Object.hasOwn (ES2022) is the modern recommendation. `in` includes inherited. `obj[key] !== undefined` fails when value is intentionally undefined.

object.question: What's the difference between == and === for objects?
options: Both compare by reference identity — `{} === {}` is false; structurally equal but different references
object.explanation: JS has no built-in deep equality. Use lodash isEqual, structuredClone for cloning, or write your own comparison.

object.question: How do you iterate own properties?
options: Object.keys/values/entries — they iterate own enumerable string keys
All work but with different scopes
object.explanation: Object.entries(obj) gives [key, value] pairs — clean for loops. for...in walks own + inherited string keys; usually filter with hasOwn.

object.question: What does Object.create(null) do?
options: Creates an object with no prototype — no toString, hasOwnProperty inherited
object.explanation: Useful as a pure key-value map. No method-name collisions with user input. Just remember it lacks default Object methods.

object.question: What's destructuring an object?
options: Pulling properties into local variables: const {name, age} = user
object.explanation: Destructuring supports defaults, renaming, and rest: const {a: localA = 0, ...others} = obj. Cleaner than repeated property access.

typeof-operator.question: What does typeof null return?
typeof-operator.explanation: Test null explicitly: value === null. typeof can't distinguish null from objects.

typeof-operator.question: What does typeof undeclaredVar return?
options: 'undefined' (typeof is the only safe access for undeclared vars)
typeof-operator.explanation: typeof is the special exception. Reading undeclaredVar otherwise throws ReferenceError. typeof on let/const in TDZ does throw.

typeof-operator.question: What does typeof function(){} return?
typeof-operator.explanation: Functions are technically callable objects, but typeof special-cases them. Useful for feature detection.

typeof-operator.question: Which type does an array return for typeof?
typeof-operator.explanation: Array.isArray is the reliable way to detect arrays. typeof returns 'object' for arrays, dates, regexes, plain objects.

typeof-operator.question: Why use typeof for feature detection in old code?
options: if (typeof Symbol !== 'undefined') ... — works without throwing for missing globals
typeof-operator.explanation: In older runtimes, accessing a missing global throws. typeof returns 'undefined' safely. Modern feature detection often uses 'in' or library polyfills.

typeof-operator.question: Does typeof distinguish between integer and float numbers?
options: No — both return 'number'. JS has a single Number type for non-bigint
typeof-operator.explanation: Use Number.isInteger to test integers. typeof can't tell Number subtypes apart.

typeof-operator.question: What does typeof 100n return?
typeof-operator.explanation: BigInt has its own type tag. Test for big integers via typeof === 'bigint'.

typeof-operator.question: What's a limitation of typeof for type-checking?
options: It can't distinguish array, date, plain object, null — they all return 'object'
typeof-operator.explanation: For finer detection, use Array.isArray, instanceof Date, or Object.prototype.toString.call(value).

typeof-operator.question: What does typeof Symbol() return?
typeof-operator.explanation: Symbols are primitives with their own type. typeof returns 'symbol' — useful for type guards in libraries that handle them.

type-casting.question: What's the difference between explicit and implicit conversion?
options: Explicit uses Number(), String(), Boolean(); implicit happens via operators (e.g., '5' - 0 → 5)
type-casting.explanation: Explicit conversions are clear in code. Implicit ones (== coercion, '+' with strings) are easy to misread — prefer explicit.

type-casting.question: What does Number('12abc') return?
options: NaN (Number requires the entire string to be a valid number)
type-casting.explanation: parseInt('12abc') returns 12 (stops at non-digit). Number is strict — full string must parse. Choose based on intent.

type-casting.question: What does String(123) produce?
type-casting.explanation: Returns the decimal string representation. Identical for numbers, but String works on null/undefined too — toString throws on those.

type-casting.question: What does +value do?
options: Coerces to Number — `+'5'` is 5; `+'5abc'` is NaN
type-casting.explanation: Unary + is a quick coercion. Equivalent to Number(value). Used in idioms like Date numeric conversion: +new Date().

type-casting.question: What does Boolean(0) return?
type-casting.explanation: All 7 falsy values become false. Everything else → true. Boolean('false') is true (non-empty string).

type-casting.question: Which is the safest pattern for converting a value to a string?
type-casting.explanation: value.toString() throws on null/undefined. String(value) handles them ('null'/'undefined'). '' + value coerces but is less explicit.

type-casting.question: What does parseInt's radix parameter do?
options: Specifies the numeric base (2-36) of the input string
type-casting.explanation: parseInt('FF', 16) → 255. Always specify radix to avoid leading-zero bugs (legacy octal interpretation in old code).

type-casting.question: What does null + 1 evaluate to?
type-casting.explanation: Coercion: null → 0, then 0 + 1 = 1. undefined + 1 → NaN (undefined coerces to NaN). Mostly avoid — use ?? for default values.

type-casting.question: What's `[] + []` in JavaScript?
options: '' (both arrays coerce to '' via toString, then string concat)
type-casting.explanation: Classic JS quirk. + with non-numbers calls valueOf/toString. Empty array .toString() → ''. The whole expression → ''.

type-casting.question: Why prefer === over == for type-checking?
options: == applies coercion rules, leading to surprises ('' == 0, [] == false). === is predictable
type-casting.explanation: Comprehensive list of == quirks runs to dozens. Use === everywhere unless intentionally checking null/undefined together (== null pattern).

data-structures.question: What's a JavaScript Map?
options: A built-in key-value collection that preserves insertion order and accepts any key type
data-structures.explanation: Map vs Object: Map keys can be any type (objects, functions, primitives), iteration is fast and ordered, .size is built-in. Pick Map for hot-path keyed lookups.

data-structures.question: What's a Set?
options: A collection of unique values — duplicates are ignored
data-structures.explanation: new Set([1,1,2]) → Set {1, 2}. Useful for deduplication: [...new Set(arr)] gives unique values.

data-structures.question: What's the typical complexity of Array.includes?
data-structures.explanation: Arrays store sequentially. For frequent membership tests on large data, a Set is O(1) — much faster.

data-structures.question: What's a WeakMap useful for?
options: Holding object keys without preventing GC — useful for metadata that should not keep targets alive
data-structures.explanation: WeakMap keys must be objects and are weakly held. When the object is GC'd, the entry vanishes. No iteration to keep things weak.

data-structures.question: What's the difference between an Array and a TypedArray?
options: Arrays are heterogeneous and dynamically sized; TypedArrays (Int32Array, etc.) hold fixed-size numeric buffers — used for binary data
data-structures.explanation: TypedArrays power Web APIs (canvas, audio, fetch responses, WebGL). Backed by ArrayBuffer for raw memory access.

data-structures.question: How are arrays implemented in JS engines?
options: Often as packed arrays (contiguous) when keys are integer-like; switch to dictionary mode for sparse/holey arrays
data-structures.explanation: Engines optimize the common case. Avoid sparse arrays (assigning index 1000 to a small array) — they de-optimize and run slower.

data-structures.question: What's a stack in JavaScript?
options: LIFO data structure — easily implemented with an array using push/pop
data-structures.explanation: Arrays serve as stacks (push/pop) and queues (push/shift, though shift is O(n)). For large queues, use a circular buffer or a library.

data-structures.question: What does JSON.stringify do with circular references?
data-structures.explanation: Circular structures (a.b = a) can't be JSON. Use a replacer or libraries like flatted/safe-json-stringify to handle them.

data-structures.question: What's the difference between Object and Map performance for frequent additions/removals?
options: Map is generally faster and more predictable for many keyed inserts/deletes
data-structures.explanation: Object's prototype chain and built-in methods can affect performance. Maps are designed for keyed operations; benchmarks usually favor Map.

data-structures.question: What's a common interview data structure question in JS?
options: LRU cache, rate limiter, debounce/throttle, deep clone — all touch Map/Set/Array semantics
data-structures.explanation: Frontend interviews lean on data structure use over implementation. Knowing when Map vs Object, Set vs Array, etc. is the practical skill tested.

arrays.question: Which method does NOT mutate the original array?
arrays.explanation: map/filter/slice/concat return new arrays. push/pop/shift/splice/sort/reverse mutate. New ES2023 methods (toSorted, toReversed) are non-mutating.

arrays.question: What does Array.prototype.map return?
options: A new array with each element transformed by the callback
arrays.explanation: Same length as source. Don't return undefined accidentally — that becomes the new value. Use forEach for side effects only.

arrays.question: What does .reduce do?
options: Folds the array into a single value via an accumulator callback
arrays.explanation: reduce((acc, cur) => ..., initial). Powerful for sums, counts, transformations to objects, etc. Skip when forEach/map is clearer.

arrays.question: How do you flatten a nested array one level?
arrays.explanation: [[1,2],[3]].flat() → [1,2,3]. flat() supports a depth argument; default is 1. flatMap = map then flat(1) in one pass.

arrays.question: What's the time complexity of .indexOf?
arrays.explanation: Walks elements until match or end. For frequent membership checks, use a Set (O(1) average).

arrays.question: What's the difference between forEach and map?
options: forEach returns undefined (side effects); map returns a new array
arrays.explanation: Use forEach for actions (logging, mutations). Use map when you need the transformed result.

arrays.question: How do you remove duplicates from an array?
options: [...new Set(arr)] — Set keeps unique values; spread back into an array
arrays.explanation: Concise and fast for primitives. For objects (deduped by identity), more work needed since {} !== {}.

arrays.question: What does .slice differ from .splice?
options: slice returns a shallow copy without mutating; splice mutates and returns the removed items
arrays.explanation: Easy mnemonic: 'slice' = scissors that copy; 'splice' = surgery that modifies. Choose carefully — interview classic.

arrays.question: How do you sort numbers correctly?
options: arr.sort((a, b) => a - b) — default sort treats elements as strings
arrays.explanation: Default sort is lexicographic. [10, 2].sort() → [10, 2] because '10' < '2' as strings. Pass a comparator for numeric sort.

arrays.question: What does spread do for arrays?
options: Expands an iterable into individual elements: [...a, ...b], or function call f(...args)
arrays.explanation: Combine arrays without mutating, copy: [...arr]. Pass array as separate args. Equivalent to apply or concat in many cases.

functions.question: What's a function declaration?
options: function f() {} — hoisted, can be called above its declaration
functions.explanation: Declarations are fully hoisted (definition included). Expressions assigned to var/let/const follow normal binding rules.

functions.question: What's an arrow function's main behavioral difference?
options: It doesn't bind its own `this`, `arguments`, or `super` — inherits them lexically
functions.explanation: Arrows are perfect for callbacks where you want the outer this. They can't be used as constructors (no `new`).

functions.question: What's a default parameter?
options: function f(x = 5) {} — uses 5 when x is undefined
functions.explanation: Defaults activate only on undefined (not null or other falsy). Each call evaluates default expressions independently — be careful with shared mutable defaults.

functions.question: What are rest parameters?
options: function f(...args) {} — collects remaining arguments into an array
functions.explanation: Replaces the legacy `arguments` (which isn't a real array). Real array means slice/map/etc. work directly.

functions.question: What's a closure?
options: A function bundled with its lexical environment — accesses outer variables after the outer function returns
functions.explanation: Closures back module patterns, currying, memoization, event handlers with state. JavaScript creates them automatically; they're foundational.

functions.question: What does Function.prototype.bind do?
options: Returns a new function with `this` (and optionally pre-applied args) fixed
functions.explanation: bind doesn't call. .call/.apply both call immediately. bind useful for passing methods as callbacks without losing this.

functions.question: What's an IIFE?
options: Immediately Invoked Function Expression: (function(){...})() — creates a private scope
functions.explanation: Pre-ES6 trick to avoid leaking variables to the global scope. Modern modules and block scope make IIFE largely unnecessary.

functions.question: What does function.length return?
options: Number of expected parameters before the first default value
functions.explanation: function f(a, b = 1, c) {} — f.length === 1. Useful for runtime overload detection (rare); mostly trivia.

functions.question: What's a higher-order function?
options: A function that takes or returns a function (e.g., map, filter, debounce, compose)
functions.explanation: Higher-order functions enable composition, currying, decorators. Most array methods are higher-order — they accept callbacks.

functions.question: What's currying?
options: Transforming a function of N args into a chain of N functions of one arg each: f(a)(b)(c)
functions.explanation: Currying enables partial application. Useful in functional patterns. Modern JS rarely curries by default; use `.bind` or arrow chains as needed.

control-flow.question: What's a guard clause?
options: Early return at the top of a function to handle invalid inputs/edge cases
control-flow.explanation: if (!user) return; reduces nesting and makes the happy path clear. A widely loved pattern.

control-flow.question: What's the difference between if/else and switch?
options: switch compares with ===, suited for many discrete values; if/else handles arbitrary conditions
control-flow.explanation: Modern JS often replaces switch with object/Map lookup tables. Switch still has ergonomic appeal for tag-based dispatch.

control-flow.question: What's a fall-through in switch?
options: When a case lacks `break`, execution continues into the next case — sometimes intentional, often a bug
control-flow.explanation: ESLint's no-fallthrough catches accidental fall-throughs. Document intentional ones with a comment.

control-flow.question: What does the ternary operator do?
options: condition ? a : b — concise inline conditional
control-flow.explanation: Great for short value choices: const label = isActive ? 'On' : 'Off'. Avoid nesting deeply — readability suffers.

control-flow.question: What does try/catch handle?
options: Synchronous throws (and awaited promise rejections in async functions)
control-flow.explanation: For non-awaited promises, attach .catch(). Don't swallow errors silently — log or rethrow.

control-flow.question: When does the `finally` block run?
options: Always — after try/catch resolves, regardless of success or thrown error
control-flow.explanation: Useful for cleanup (closing connections, resetting state). Even works with promises (Promise.prototype.finally).

control-flow.question: What's an early return?
options: Returning before the end of the function — common for guard clauses
control-flow.explanation: Reduces indentation, clarifies preconditions. Functional style prefers single returns; pragmatic style favors early returns for readability.

control-flow.question: What does the optional `do-while` loop guarantee?
options: The loop body runs at least once before the condition is checked
control-flow.explanation: Use when you need at least one execution (e.g., prompting a user until input is valid). Less common than while/for.

control-flow.question: What does `break` do in a loop?
control-flow.explanation: continue skips current iteration. break ends the loop. Both work in for/while; break also exits switch.

control-flow.question: What's structured concurrency in async control flow?
options: Patterns/abortControllers that ensure spawned tasks have well-defined lifetimes — cancellable, awaitable
control-flow.explanation: AbortController + signals lets fetch and async tasks be cancelled cleanly when their parent context unmounts or times out.

loops-and-iterations.question: Which loop iterates an iterable's values?
loops-and-iterations.explanation: for...of iterates iterables (Array, Map, Set, generators, strings, NodeList). for...in iterates object string keys.

loops-and-iterations.question: Why prefer .map over for-loops for transformations?
options: More declarative — intent is clear, returns a new array, easier to chain
loops-and-iterations.explanation: for-loops are imperative. map/filter/reduce express intent. Use loops when you need early break/continue or maximum perf.

loops-and-iterations.question: What does break vs continue do in a loop?
options: break exits the loop; continue skips to the next iteration
loops-and-iterations.explanation: break is also valid in switch. continue jumps to the loop condition (or update step in for-loops).

loops-and-iterations.question: How do you iterate a Map?
options: for (const [k, v] of map) — Maps are iterable; entries by default
loops-and-iterations.explanation: Both work. for...of with destructuring is concise. forEach is method-style. Maps preserve insertion order.

loops-and-iterations.question: Should you `await` inside a forEach callback?
options: No — forEach ignores the promise; use a for-of loop or Promise.all/map
loops-and-iterations.explanation: forEach doesn't await. Use for (const x of arr) await ... for sequential async, or Promise.all(arr.map(async f)) for parallel.

loops-and-iterations.question: What's a labeled loop?
options: label: for (...) { break label; } — break/continue can target an outer loop
loops-and-iterations.explanation: Rare but useful for nested loops. break label exits the labeled loop; continue label moves to its next iteration.

loops-and-iterations.question: What's the typical complexity gotcha when iterating array.length inside a loop?
options: Reading length on each iteration is fine for normal arrays; mutating during iteration leads to bugs
