asymptotic-notation.question: What does asymptotic mean in CS?
options: Behavior as input size approaches infinity — captures growth rate, not exact runtime
asymptotic-notation.explanation: Constants and small inputs are ignored. The point is: as n grows, what's the dominant cost? Useful for comparing algorithms.

asymptotic-notation.question: What's Big-O?
options: Upper bound on growth — algorithm runs at most this fast (asymptotically)
asymptotic-notation.explanation: f(n) = O(g(n)) means f grows no faster than some constant times g for large n.

asymptotic-notation.question: What's Big-Ω (Omega)?
options: Lower bound — algorithm runs at least this fast
asymptotic-notation.explanation: Often the easier-to-prove bound. f(n) = Ω(g(n)) means f grows at least as fast as g for large n.

asymptotic-notation.question: What's Big-Θ (Theta)?
options: Tight bound — both upper and lower; growth is exactly proportional to g(n)
asymptotic-notation.explanation: f(n) = Θ(g(n)) means there exist constants c₁, c₂ where c₁g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c₂g(n) for large n. The strongest bound.

asymptotic-notation.question: Which is most commonly used in practice?
options: Big-O — describes worst-case growth, simplest to compute and compare
asymptotic-notation.explanation: When people say 'this is O(n log n)', they usually mean theta (tight) — but the convention is to write O for any upper bound.

asymptotic-notation.question: Is O(n) ⊂ O(n²)?
options: Yes — anything that's O(n) is also O(n²) (just a looser bound)
asymptotic-notation.explanation: O is an upper bound. n ≤ n² for n ≥ 1, so any O(n) algorithm is technically also O(n²). For tightness, use Θ.

asymptotic-notation.question: What does little-o (o(n)) mean?
options: Strictly less than — f grows strictly slower than g
asymptotic-notation.explanation: Less common. f(n) = o(g(n)) means f/g → 0 as n → ∞. Useful for refining upper bounds.

asymptotic-notation.question: Why do we drop constants?
options: Because hardware-dependent constants don't change the algorithm's asymptotic behavior
asymptotic-notation.explanation: 1000n + 5 and 2n + 100 are both O(n). The constant differences shrink relative to growth at large n.

asymptotic-notation.question: Common pitfall in asymptotic analysis?
options: Forgetting that asymptotic notation hides constants — for small n, an O(n²) algorithm can beat an O(n log n)
asymptotic-notation.explanation: Real algorithms have constants. Insertion sort beats mergesort below ~30 elements — std libs use hybrid sorts that switch between them.

asymptotic-notation.question: What's the difference between worst, average, best case in big-O?
options: Big-O usually refers to worst-case unless stated; average and best are useful but typically less actionable
asymptotic-notation.explanation: Worst case gives the safety guarantee. Quicksort: average O(n log n), worst O(n²). For SLAs, worst case matters.

big-o-notation.question: What does O(1) mean?
options: Constant time — independent of input size
big-o-notation.explanation: Examples: array index, hash map lookup average, push/pop on stack. Doesn't mean 'fast' but 'doesn't depend on n'.

big-o-notation.question: Time complexity of finding an element in an unsorted array?
big-o-notation.explanation: Worst case: walk the whole array. Sorted arrays allow binary search O(log n). Hash sets allow O(1) average.

big-o-notation.question: Inserting at the front of an array?
big-o-notation.explanation: Linked lists do this in O(1). For arrays, prefer pushing at the end and (if needed) reversing once.

big-o-notation.question: Sorting comparison-based algorithms cannot do better than?
options: O(n log n) — proven lower bound for comparison sorts
big-o-notation.explanation: Mergesort, heapsort, quicksort hit this bound. O(n) sorts (counting, radix) require non-comparison-based techniques.

big-o-notation.question: What's O(n!)?
options: Factorial growth — usually too slow for n>10 (e.g., trying all permutations)
big-o-notation.explanation: Brute-force traveling salesman is O(n!). Solutions: DP (O(n² 2ⁿ) Held-Karp), heuristics, approximation.

big-o-notation.question: What's the complexity of binary search?
big-o-notation.explanation: Halves the search space each step. log₂(n) iterations. Requires sorted input.

big-o-notation.question: Can two algorithms have the same Big-O but different real performance?
options: Yes — constants and cache behavior differ. Big-O is a guide, not a guarantee
big-o-notation.explanation: O(n) with cache-unfriendly random access is slower than O(n) sequential scan. Profile real workloads when constants matter.

big-o-notation.question: What does 'amortized O(1)' mean?
options: Average cost per op is O(1) over a sequence, even if individual ops can be slower
big-o-notation.explanation: Dynamic array push: occasional resize is O(n), but distributed across n inserts → amortized O(1).

big-o-notation.question: When can simple algorithms beat fancy ones in Big-O?
options: Small n, simple structure, cache-friendly access — small constants matter
big-o-notation.explanation: Insertion sort vs mergesort below ~30 elements. Linear scan vs hash map lookup for tiny lookups (cache vs allocation overhead).

big-o-notation.question: What's the practical advice on Big-O?
options: Aim for the right asymptotic class; profile real workloads when speed matters
big-o-notation.explanation: Algorithm choice sets the ceiling. Implementation determines the constant. Both matter; Big-O dominates at scale.

big-theta-notation.question: What does Θ(n) mean?
options: Tight bound — algorithm grows exactly proportional to n (both upper and lower)
big-theta-notation.explanation: Θ is stricter than O. Θ(n) means the algorithm runs in linear time, not just at most linear time.

big-theta-notation.question: When is Θ more useful than O?
options: When you need to communicate the exact growth rate, not just an upper bound
big-theta-notation.explanation: Saying mergesort is O(n²) is technically correct but misleading. Θ(n log n) is precise and informative.

big-theta-notation.question: What's the relationship: Θ(g) = O(g) ∩ Ω(g)?
options: True — tight bound is upper AND lower bound combined
big-theta-notation.explanation: Θ(g) means f grows at the same rate as g (bounded both above and below by constant multiples of g).

big-theta-notation.question: Why might researchers prefer Θ in papers?
options: Precise communication of an algorithm's complexity, easier comparison
big-theta-notation.explanation: Academic CS literature often uses Θ to be exact. Industry engineers tend to use O loosely (typically meaning Θ).

big-theta-notation.question: What's a Θ(1) example?
options: Hash map lookup average, array index, push/pop
big-theta-notation.explanation: Constant time. Note worst-case hash map is Θ(n) due to collisions; the constant claim is for average-case under good hashing.

big-theta-notation.question: Linear search worst case is Θ(?)
options: n — must walk all n elements when target is absent
big-theta-notation.explanation: Both upper and lower bounds are linear in the worst case. Average case (uniform target distribution) is also Θ(n).

big-theta-notation.question: Mergesort is Θ(?)
options: n log n — same upper and lower bound regardless of input
big-theta-notation.explanation: Mergesort's Θ(n log n) holds for any input. Quicksort is Θ(n log n) average, Θ(n²) worst — different per-input behavior.

big-theta-notation.question: Can you prove Θ(g) directly?
options: Often by showing both ≤ and ≥ bounds, or by exact counting
big-theta-notation.explanation: Master Theorem and recurrence solving give Θ bounds. Counting operations + dominant term gives Θ for explicit code.

big-theta-notation.question: What does 'tight' mean in tight bound?
options: The bound matches the algorithm's behavior — no slack above or below
big-theta-notation.explanation: A non-tight upper bound (O(n²) for an O(n) algorithm) is true but uninformative. Tight bounds = honest complexity.

big-theta-notation.question: When can Θ be hard to determine?
options: When worst and best cases differ significantly — quicksort, hash table operations
big-theta-notation.explanation: Sometimes only an O bound is provable. For algorithms where Θ doesn't apply uniformly, give worst/average/best separately.

big-omega-notation.question: What does Ω(n) mean?
options: Lower bound — algorithm runs at least this fast (or at least this slow, asymptotically)
big-omega-notation.explanation: Often used to prove minimum work required. Sorting comparison-based: Ω(n log n) — no algorithm can be faster.

big-omega-notation.question: Why is Ω useful for proving lower bounds?
options: It establishes that no algorithm in a class can beat this growth rate — fundamental theory
big-omega-notation.explanation: Comparison-based sort lower bound: Ω(n log n). Implies you must move beyond comparisons for faster sorts (counting, radix).

big-omega-notation.question: Linear search best case is Ω(?)
big-omega-notation.explanation: Best case Ω(1). Worst case O(n). Tight bound Θ doesn't apply because best/worst differ.

big-omega-notation.question: What's the relationship between O and Ω?
big-omega-notation.explanation: If f grows at most as fast as g, then g grows at least as fast as f. Symmetric definitions.

big-omega-notation.question: Why is Ω used less often than O in practice?
options: Engineers care about worst-case performance (O); theoretical analysis uses Ω for lower-bound proofs
big-omega-notation.explanation: When designing algorithms, you want guarantees on the upper end. When proving 'this is the best we can do', Ω matters.

big-omega-notation.question: Sorting integers with counting sort is Ω(?)
options: n + k where k is the value range — beats comparison-sort lower bound by avoiding comparisons
big-omega-notation.explanation: Counting sort uses array indexing instead of comparisons. Linear in n + k — doesn't violate Ω(n log n) for comparison sorts because it's not comparison-based.

big-omega-notation.question: Can an algorithm be Ω(2ⁿ)?
options: Yes — exhaustive search of all subsets is Ω(2ⁿ) regardless of optimization
big-omega-notation.explanation: Some problems inherently require exponential work in the worst case. Approximation/heuristic algorithms may run faster but give non-optimal answers.

big-omega-notation.question: What's the lower bound on accessing an arbitrary element in an unsorted unindexed structure?
options: Ω(n) — must inspect each element in the worst case
big-omega-notation.explanation: Without indexing/sorting, no shortcuts exist. Hash tables index implicitly via hashing → Ω(1) average.

big-omega-notation.question: What's the difference between Ω and o?
options: Ω is non-strict (≥); o is strict (<). Both refer to lower-bound directions but with different tightness
big-omega-notation.explanation: f = ω(g) means f grows strictly faster than g. Less common in practice but precise.

big-omega-notation.question: What's a practical interview tip for Ω?
options: Mention 'best-case Ω(1)' or similar to show theoretical rigor when relevant
big-omega-notation.explanation: Sometimes interviewers ask 'is your algorithm optimal?' — answering with the lower bound (Ω) shows depth of understanding.

common-runtimes.question: Order from fastest to slowest growth:
options: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(2ⁿ) < O(n!)
common-runtimes.explanation: Memorize this order. Anything above O(n²) is suspect for large inputs.

common-runtimes.question: Which algorithms are typically O(log n)?
options: Binary search, balanced BST operations, heap operations
common-runtimes.explanation: Common pattern: halve the search space. Operates on sorted/structured data.

common-runtimes.question: Which algorithms are O(n log n)?
options: Mergesort, heapsort, quicksort (avg), efficient comparison-based sorts
common-runtimes.explanation: Best comparison-sort runtime. Typical lower bound for many divide-and-conquer algorithms.

common-runtimes.question: Which is typically O(n²)?
options: Bubble sort, insertion sort, naive nested-loop algorithms
common-runtimes.explanation: Two nested loops over n. Brute force pair-checking. Watch for opportunities to drop one factor of n via hashing or sorting.

common-runtimes.question: When would O(2ⁿ) be acceptable?
options: Small n (≤ 25), exhaustive search problems, NP-hard with no better known algorithm
common-runtimes.explanation: Subset enumeration, brute-force satisfiability, etc. For larger n, look for DP, branch-and-bound, or approximation.

common-runtimes.question: Where do O(n!) algorithms appear?
common-runtimes.explanation: Factorial usually means 'try every permutation'. For n=10, that's 3.6M; for n=15, over a trillion. Beyond ~12 use DP.

common-runtimes.question: At what input size does O(n²) become problematic?
options: Around 10⁴-10⁵ where each operation is non-trivial; depends on hardware
common-runtimes.explanation: n=10⁵ gives 10¹⁰ ops — too slow on a single machine in real time. n=10⁴ is borderline; n=10³ usually fine.

common-runtimes.question: Why does O(n log n) feel 'almost linear' for most inputs?
options: log n grows very slowly — log₂(10⁹) ≈ 30, so n log n ≈ 30n
common-runtimes.explanation: log factor adds 20-30x for typical large inputs — manageable. Many real-world algorithms aim for O(n log n).

common-runtimes.question: Which is faster: O(n²) or O(n^1.5)?
common-runtimes.explanation: Algorithms with subquadratic runtimes (e.g., shellsort O(n^1.5) for some gaps) beat n² eventually. Specific exponent matters.

common-runtimes.question: What's the takeaway about runtime classes?
options: Recognize them quickly to identify whether your algorithm will scale
common-runtimes.explanation: Pattern recognition is the skill. Once you see a problem and know which runtime class fits, the rest is implementation.

constant.question: What does O(1) mean?
options: Constant time — independent of input size
constant.explanation: Operations like array index, hash lookup average, push/pop on stack. The actual time may be 100ns or 1μs — the point is it doesn't grow with n.

constant.question: Examples of O(1) operations?
constant.explanation: Direct lookups via index or hash. Conceptually a single computation regardless of data size.

constant.question: Is O(1) always faster than O(n) for small inputs?
options: Not necessarily — constants matter; O(1) hash lookup may have higher constant than O(n) walk for n=3
constant.explanation: Big-O ignores constants. For very small n, simple algorithms can outperform 'optimal' ones with overhead.

constant.question: Why aim for O(1) when possible?
options: Operations don't get slower as data grows — predictable, scalable
constant.explanation: Database design, hot-path code, real-time systems — O(1) gives consistent latency. Foundation of cache and hash table design.

constant.question: Is array.length O(1)?
options: Yes — modern languages store length as a property
constant.explanation: Counting elements in a singly linked list is O(n) (must walk). Arrays maintain length explicitly — O(1) read.

constant.question: What's worst case for hash map get?
options: O(n) when all keys collide; O(1) average with good hash
constant.explanation: In practice you can rely on average. Worst case matters for adversarial inputs (hash flooding) — modern impls defend with randomized hashes.

constant.question: Common O(1) data structure operations?
options: Stack push/pop, queue enqueue/dequeue (with deque), hash map insert/get/delete avg
constant.explanation: Foundations of efficient algorithms. Most problems break down into combinations of these primitives.

constant.question: What's the gotcha with 'O(1) amortized'?
options: Average over a sequence — individual ops can be slower (e.g., dynamic array resize is O(n))
constant.explanation: Amortized O(1) is fine for most use cases. Real-time systems may need worst-case O(1) (use static structures or special algorithms).

constant.question: Why does cache locality matter even for O(1) ops?
options: Hash map lookups can miss cache; sequential array accesses hit it — same Big-O, vastly different real performance
constant.explanation: Memory hierarchy: L1 cache 1ns, RAM 100ns. O(1) random access can be 100x slower than O(1) sequential access in practice.

constant.question: Example of O(1) space?
options: Two-pointer in-place reverse — uses fixed extra variables regardless of input size
constant.explanation: In-place algorithms use O(1) extra space. Important when memory is constrained.

logarithmic.question: What's O(log n)?
options: Logarithmic — input size halving each step (or doubling) gives log iterations
logarithmic.explanation: log₂(10⁶) ≈ 20. log₂(10⁹) ≈ 30. Logarithms grow very slowly — basically constant for practical inputs.

logarithmic.question: Classic O(log n) algorithm?
logarithmic.explanation: Each step halves the search space. log₂(n) iterations to find target. Foundation of efficient sorted-data lookup.

logarithmic.question: Balanced binary search tree operations?
logarithmic.explanation: BSTs (AVL, red-black) maintain balance, keeping height log n. Languages: Java TreeMap, C++ std::map, Python sortedcontainers.

logarithmic.question: Heap operations?
options: O(log n) push and pop; O(1) peek
logarithmic.explanation: Binary heap: complete tree of height log n. Sift-up/sift-down each take log steps. Perfect for priority queues.

logarithmic.question: Why is log base unimportant in Big-O?
options: All log bases differ by a constant: log₂(n) = log_b(n) × constant — Big-O drops constants
logarithmic.explanation: log₂, log₁₀, ln are all O(log n). Implementations may use base 2, 10, or e — asymptotic class is identical.

logarithmic.question: Example of O(log n) iteration pattern?
logarithmic.explanation: Doubling/halving = logarithmic. Spotting it in code is a key skill: i *= 2, n /= 2, recursion on halves.

logarithmic.question: What's the height of a balanced BST?
logarithmic.explanation: Balanced trees maintain log-height by construction. Unbalanced (e.g., insert sorted into vanilla BST) degrades to O(n).

logarithmic.question: When does log n appear in recursion?
options: When the problem halves at each level: T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) → O(log n)
logarithmic.explanation: Master theorem case 2 with linear cost gives n log n; constant cost gives just log n.

logarithmic.question: Is O(log log n) faster than O(log n)?
options: Yes — log of a log grows extremely slowly. Real for some advanced algorithms
logarithmic.explanation: log log n is essentially 5-6 for any practical n. Niche but real (e.g., van Emde Boas trees).

logarithmic.question: Why are O(log n) algorithms desirable?
options: Scale to huge inputs gracefully — logarithmic time means doubling input adds only a constant
logarithmic.explanation: Doubling n adds 1 to log n. Going from a billion to a trillion items adds maybe 10 operations. Magical.

linear.question: What's O(n) complexity?
options: Linear — runtime grows in direct proportion to input size
linear.explanation: Doubling input doubles runtime. Common for single-pass algorithms: count, sum, find max, copy.

linear.question: Linear search complexity?
options: O(n) worst case (target not found or at the end)
linear.explanation: Walks each element until match. O(n) average if target uniformly distributed. O(1) if target is always first (rare).

linear.question: Sum of an array?
linear.explanation: Visit each element once. Could parallelize across CPUs/threads, but the total work is still O(n).

linear.question: Why is O(n) often optimal for many problems?
options: Many problems require seeing every input at least once — Ω(n)
linear.explanation: Lower bound Ω(n) for problems like 'sum all elements' or 'find max'. You can't do better than touching everything once.

linear.question: Two passes over n?
options: O(n) — sequential operations of same Big-O collapse
linear.explanation: n + n = 2n → drop constant → O(n). Three passes still O(n). Multiple sequential passes don't change complexity class.

linear.question: Example of converting O(n²) to O(n)?
options: Use a hash set: 'two sum' problem goes from nested loop to single pass with O(1) lookups
linear.explanation: Many quadratic-looking problems become linear with the right data structure. Hash maps are the most common tool.

linear.question: What's Kadane's algorithm complexity?
options: O(n) — single pass to find max subarray sum
linear.explanation: Kadane: dp[i] = max(arr[i], dp[i-1] + arr[i]). Track running max. Beats O(n³) brute force, O(n²) DP.

linear.question: Linear time space?
linear.explanation: Building a sorted copy, hash set of all elements, prefix sum array — all O(n) space. Often a fair trade for O(n) time gains.

linear.question: What's tail call optimization's role?
options: Allows recursive functions ending in a call to reuse the stack frame — turning O(n) stack into O(1)
linear.explanation: Major in functional languages. Most JS engines do not implement TCO despite ES6 spec. Convert to iteration when stack depth could be issue.

linear.question: Linear-time sorting possible?
options: Yes for non-comparison sorts: counting sort O(n + k), radix sort O(nk)
linear.explanation: Counting sort if values are small integers. Radix sort for fixed-width keys. Comparison-based lower bound is O(n log n).

polynomial.question: What's polynomial time?
options: O(n^k) for some constant k — n², n³, etc.
polynomial.explanation: P (polynomial time) is the class of problems solvable in polynomial time. Distinct from NP-hard problems requiring exponential time (in worst case).

polynomial.question: What's a typical O(n²) algorithm?
options: Bubble sort, insertion sort, selection sort, naive matrix-vector mult
polynomial.explanation: Two nested loops over n. For small n it's fine. For n=10⁵, 10¹⁰ operations is too slow for typical 1-sec budget.

polynomial.question: When is O(n²) acceptable?
options: Small input (n ≤ 1000-10000), simple structure, when better algorithms aren't worth the complexity
polynomial.explanation: Pragmatism: insertion sort beats mergesort for small arrays. Don't over-engineer. Reach for n log n when n grows.

polynomial.question: What does O(n³) typically come from?
options: Three nested loops or matrix multiplication
polynomial.explanation: Matrix multiplication naive is O(n³). Strassen's is O(n^2.81). Often interview problems have O(n³) brute-force solutions reducible with cleverness.

polynomial.question: What's the difference between polynomial and exponential complexity?
options: Polynomial: n^k for fixed k. Exponential: k^n — unbounded in n
polynomial.explanation: Exponential explodes much faster. n=20: 20² = 400, 2²⁰ = 1M. n=50: 50² = 2500, 2⁵⁰ ≈ 10¹⁵.

polynomial.question: Are O(n²) and O(n²·⁵) both polynomial?
options: Yes — any polynomial exponent counts as polynomial complexity
polynomial.explanation: Polynomial means O(n^c) for some constant c. Even fractional exponents qualify. Distinguishes from exponential or factorial growth.

polynomial.question: Common O(n²) reduction technique?
options: Hash sets, sorting, sliding window, two-pointer — eliminate one loop dimension
polynomial.explanation: Many quadratic problems have linear or n log n solutions with the right structure. Pattern recognition is key.

polynomial.question: Is O(n^100) polynomial?
options: Yes technically — but practically slower than O(2ⁿ) for small n. Constant in exponent matters
polynomial.explanation: Theoretical CS calls anything polynomial 'tractable'. In practice, n^100 isn't useful. Engineering cares about small constants.

polynomial.question: Can polynomial-time algorithms be fast in practice?
options: Yes for low-degree polynomials — O(n), O(n log n), even O(n²) for medium inputs
polynomial.explanation: n log n algorithms power most production systems. n² is fine for moderate sizes. Pragmatic engineering: pick the simplest sufficient algorithm.

polynomial.question: Why care about the distinction polynomial vs exponential?
options: P vs NP — fundamental separation between tractable and (likely) intractable problems
polynomial.explanation: Million-dollar Clay Institute problem. NP-hard problems (TSP, SAT) have no known polynomial-time solution; P=NP would change CS forever.

exponential.question: What's O(2ⁿ)?
options: Exponential — doubling input squares the runtime
exponential.explanation: n=10: 1024. n=30: 1 billion. n=60: more than atoms in observable universe. Hits walls fast.

exponential.question: Classic O(2ⁿ) algorithm?
options: Naive recursive Fibonacci, exhaustive subset enumeration, brute-force SAT
exponential.explanation: Naive Fib(n) = Fib(n-1) + Fib(n-2) → tree of calls, O(2ⁿ). Memoization fixes it to O(n).

exponential.question: When is O(2ⁿ) acceptable?
options: Very small n (≤ 25-30), or when problem has no known better algorithm
exponential.explanation: Subset enumeration for n=20 gives ~1M — fine. n=30: 1B, slow. Beyond that look for DP, branch-and-bound, approximation.

exponential.question: How do you reduce O(2ⁿ) to polynomial often?
options: Memoization/DP — cache subproblems to avoid recomputation
exponential.explanation: Many recursive solutions revisit the same state. Caching turns 2ⁿ into a polynomial number of states with O(1) work each.

exponential.question: What's the recurrence for O(2ⁿ)?
options: T(n) = 2T(n-1) + O(1) — typical of binary recursion
exponential.explanation: Two recursive calls per level → 2ⁿ leaves. Each level has O(1) work in this form (constant per call).

exponential.question: Is 3ⁿ also exponential?
options: Yes — anything with a constant base raised to n is exponential, just slower or faster than 2ⁿ
exponential.explanation: Branching factor matters: with 3 choices per step, n=20 gives 3.5 billion. Higher base, faster explosion.

exponential.question: Why are exponential algorithms still studied?
options: Some problems (NP-hard) likely have no polynomial-time algorithm; exponential is the best known
exponential.explanation: TSP, SAT, k-coloring — fundamental NP-hard problems. Best known algorithms are exponential or sub-exponential. Heuristics often used in practice.

exponential.question: Can pruning save exponential algorithms?
options: Yes — branch-and-bound, memoization, constraint propagation can dramatically cut the explored tree
exponential.explanation: Worst case still exponential, but average case can be dramatically faster. Real-world solvers (SAT, ILP) are highly optimized despite exponential theory.

exponential.question: What does 'pseudo-polynomial' mean?
options: Polynomial in numeric value, not bit length — knapsack DP is O(nW), polynomial in W which is exponential in input size
exponential.explanation: Knapsack DP runtime depends on capacity. Capacity 10⁹ needs 10⁹ work — polynomial in W but W is exponential in its bit representation.

exponential.question: Example of converting exponential to polynomial via DP?
options: Fibonacci, longest common subsequence, edit distance, knapsack — DP gives polynomial time
exponential.explanation: Recognize overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure. Memoize. Many DP problems have natural recursive O(2ⁿ) versions.

factorial.question: What's O(n!)?
factorial.explanation: Beats exponential. n=10: 3.6M. n=12: 479M. n=15: 1.3 trillion. Above n=12 typically infeasible.

factorial.question: Classic O(n!) problem?
options: Generating all permutations of n elements
factorial.explanation: n elements → n! arrangements. Used in brute-force traveling salesman, anagram-related problems.

factorial.question: Why is O(n!) feared?
options: Tiny input changes explode runtime — n=15 is already 13 trillion
factorial.explanation: Stirling's approximation: n! ≈ √(2πn) × (n/e)ⁿ. Even compared to 2ⁿ, factorial pulls ahead fast.

factorial.question: How do you avoid factorial complexity?
options: DP over states (Held-Karp TSP O(n² 2ⁿ)), pruning, branch-and-bound, approximation
factorial.explanation: Held-Karp reduces TSP from O(n!) to O(n² 2ⁿ) — still exponential but n=20 is now ~400M, doable.

factorial.question: Generating permutations recursively is O(?)
options: O(n × n!) — n! permutations × O(n) to record each
factorial.explanation: Many algorithms operating on all permutations cost slightly more than n! due to per-permutation work.

factorial.question: Brute-force traveling salesman is O(?)
factorial.explanation: n! orderings; check each against constraints. Held-Karp DP improves to O(n² 2ⁿ). Approximation algorithms achieve provable bounds in polynomial time.

factorial.question: When is brute-force factorial okay?
options: Tiny n (≤ 8-10), or as a baseline before optimizing
factorial.explanation: Useful for small puzzles, exhaustive analysis, or as a fallback when correctness matters more than speed.

factorial.question: Stirling's approximation tells us n! is O(?)
factorial.explanation: Useful for asymptotic comparisons. n! grows roughly as nⁿ × something — clearly worse than 2ⁿ.

factorial.question: Can heuristics beat O(n!) in practice?
options: Yes — for many factorial problems (TSP, scheduling), heuristics give good-enough answers in polynomial time
factorial.explanation: Genetic algorithms, simulated annealing, A* — give near-optimal results in seconds for problems brute force can't solve in a lifetime.

factorial.question: What's the real-world advice on factorial problems?
options: Recognize them, then choose: small enough to brute force? polynomial-time approximation? exponential DP?
factorial.explanation: n=10: brute force fine. n=20: DP if exists. n=100: approximation. Match technique to problem size and accuracy needs.

sorting-algorithms.question: What's the lower bound for comparison-based sorting?
options: Ω(n log n) — proven by decision tree analysis
sorting-algorithms.explanation: n! possible orderings → decision tree height log(n!) = Θ(n log n). Mergesort, heapsort match this. Quicksort matches on average.

sorting-algorithms.question: Is mergesort stable?
options: Yes — preserves relative order of equal elements
sorting-algorithms.explanation: Stability matters when sorting by multiple keys. Java's Arrays.sort uses TimSort (stable). Quicksort is generally not stable.

sorting-algorithms.question: Quicksort's worst case?
options: O(n²) — already-sorted with bad pivot choice
sorting-algorithms.explanation: Mitigated by randomized pivots or median-of-three. Average and best cases are O(n log n).

sorting-algorithms.question: Which sorts are O(n) in best case for nearly-sorted input?
options: Insertion sort, TimSort, Bubble sort with early-exit
sorting-algorithms.explanation: Adaptive sorts detect existing order. TimSort (Python's sorted, Java's Arrays.sort) is highly adaptive — used in real systems.

sorting-algorithms.question: Is heapsort in-place?
options: Yes — uses O(1) extra space (besides input array)
sorting-algorithms.explanation: Heapsort builds a heap in-place and extracts max repeatedly. Useful when memory is tight. Mergesort needs O(n) auxiliary space.

sorting-algorithms.question: Counting sort complexity?
options: O(n + k) where k is value range — non-comparison-based
sorting-algorithms.explanation: Beats Ω(n log n) by avoiding comparisons. Suited for small integer ranges. Radix sort uses counting sort as a subroutine.

sorting-algorithms.question: Best general-purpose comparison sort in practice?
options: TimSort or IntroSort — hybrid algorithms used by std libs
sorting-algorithms.explanation: TimSort: stable, adaptive, O(n log n). IntroSort: quicksort that switches to heapsort on bad pivots. Stdlib choice matters less than 'use the stdlib'.

sorting-algorithms.question: When is bubble sort acceptable?
options: Tiny lists, teaching examples, or when simplicity > speed
sorting-algorithms.explanation: O(n²) average. Easy to reason about and debug. Real code should use stdlib sort almost always.

sorting-algorithms.question: What's external sorting?
options: Sorting data too large for memory — chunks sorted on disk, then merged
sorting-algorithms.explanation: Used for terabyte-scale data. Read chunks, sort in memory, write back. Then merge sorted runs (k-way merge) into final output.

sorting-algorithms.question: Should you implement sort yourself in production?
options: No — use stdlib (Array.sort, Arrays.sort, std::sort) — battle-tested and optimized
sorting-algorithms.explanation: Implement once for learning. In production, stdlib does the job. Implementing your own risks bugs and underperformance.

bubble-sort.question: What's bubble sort's idea?
options: Repeatedly swap adjacent out-of-order elements; largest 'bubbles' to the end each pass
bubble-sort.explanation: After pass 1, max is at end. After pass 2, second max is at second-to-last. Stops when no swaps needed.

bubble-sort.question: Bubble sort's average complexity?
bubble-sort.explanation: Two nested loops over n. n × n / 2 comparisons. Slow for large input, but easy to teach.

bubble-sort.question: Bubble sort's best case?
options: O(n) — already sorted, with early-exit when no swaps occur
bubble-sort.explanation: Add a 'swapped' flag. If false after a full pass, the array is sorted — break. Linear time on already-sorted input.

bubble-sort.question: Is bubble sort stable?
options: Yes — equal elements don't swap positions
bubble-sort.explanation: Adjacent swaps only when strictly out of order. Equal elements stay in original order. Useful for multi-key sorts.

bubble-sort.question: Bubble sort space complexity?
bubble-sort.explanation: Sorts in place using only a few index variables. No auxiliary arrays needed.

bubble-sort.question: When is bubble sort acceptable?
options: Tiny n (10s), teaching examples, or when simplicity matters more than speed
bubble-sort.explanation: Real code should use stdlib sort. Bubble sort has narrow practical applicability outside of education.

bubble-sort.question: Bubble vs selection sort?
options: Both O(n²); bubble is stable, selection is not (in typical impl)
bubble-sort.explanation: Selection sort does fewer swaps (n total) but more comparisons. Bubble can early-exit on sorted input.

bubble-sort.question: Bubble vs insertion sort?
options: Insertion sort typically faster in practice — fewer assignments per pass and adaptive
bubble-sort.explanation: Insertion sort shifts instead of swapping. On nearly-sorted input, both are O(n) but insertion has smaller constants.

bubble-sort.question: Is bubble sort used in any modern language stdlib?
bubble-sort.explanation: Modern stdlibs use sophisticated hybrid sorts. Bubble sort is purely educational.

bubble-sort.question: What's a bubble sort optimization?
options: Track last swap position; everything after it is sorted — reduce inner loop bound each pass
bubble-sort.explanation: Some passes settle a large portion. Tracking 'last swap index' tightens the upper bound, saving comparisons in subsequent passes.

merge-sort.question: What's mergesort's complexity?
options: O(n log n) — guaranteed in best, average, and worst cases
merge-sort.explanation: Divide into halves (log n levels) × linear merge per level (n) = O(n log n). Predictable performance regardless of input.

merge-sort.question: Is mergesort stable?
options: Yes — preserves relative order of equal elements (when implemented correctly)
merge-sort.explanation: When merging, if elements are equal, take from the left subarray first — preserves their original order. Important for multi-key sorts.

merge-sort.question: Mergesort's space complexity?
options: O(n) — needs temporary array for merging
merge-sort.explanation: Standard mergesort allocates auxiliary arrays. In-place mergesort exists but is much slower and complex. Quicksort wins on space (O(log n)).

merge-sort.question: Mergesort works well for?
options: Linked lists (no random access needed) and external sorting (large data)
merge-sort.explanation: Merging linked lists is natural — no extra space needed. External sort uses chunked mergesort to handle data larger than memory.

merge-sort.question: Mergesort's recurrence?
merge-sort.explanation: Master theorem: a=2, b=2, f(n)=n. Comparing log_b(a) = 1 with f's exponent → case 2 → Θ(n log n).

merge-sort.question: Bottom-up vs top-down mergesort?
options: Top-down: recursive, divides; bottom-up: iterative, merges runs of size 1, 2, 4, ...
merge-sort.explanation: Bottom-up avoids recursion overhead and is the basis of TimSort (which detects natural runs in input).

merge-sort.question: When pick mergesort over quicksort?
options: Stable sort needed, predictable O(n log n) required, sorting linked lists, external sort
merge-sort.explanation: Quicksort is faster on average due to lower constant factors and cache friendliness, but mergesort gives guarantees quicksort doesn't.

merge-sort.question: Mergesort on already-sorted input?
options: Still O(n log n) — doesn't adapt to existing order
merge-sort.explanation: Pure mergesort isn't adaptive. TimSort detects runs and skips merging within them, achieving O(n) best case for sorted input.

merge-sort.question: What does TimSort do differently?
options: Detects 'runs' of already-sorted subsequences and merges them — adaptive, stable, O(n log n)
merge-sort.explanation: Default sort in Python (Timsort) and Java (Arrays.sort for objects). Excels on real-world partially-sorted data.

merge-sort.question: Standard library sort in JS — what is it?
options: Engine-defined (V8 uses TimSort since 2018; older was QuickSort) — stable, O(n log n)
merge-sort.explanation: Modern V8 uses TimSort which is stable. ECMAScript spec required stability since ES2019. Use Array.prototype.sort with confidence.

insertion-sort.question: What's insertion sort's idea?
options: Build sorted prefix; insert each next element into its correct position by shifting
insertion-sort.explanation: Like sorting playing cards in your hand. Take next card, slide it left into the sorted section. Adaptive and intuitive.

insertion-sort.question: Insertion sort's average complexity?
insertion-sort.explanation: Two nested loops — outer for elements, inner for shift. Quadratic for random input. Best case O(n) for sorted input.

insertion-sort.question: Best case for insertion sort?
insertion-sort.explanation: Each new element compares once and stays. Linear scan with no shifts. Highly adaptive — beats mergesort on near-sorted input.

insertion-sort.question: Is insertion sort stable?
insertion-sort.explanation: Equal elements don't swap. Preserves input order — important for multi-key sorts.

insertion-sort.question: Insertion sort space?
insertion-sort.explanation: Sorts in place. Useful when memory is constrained or data is already in an array.

insertion-sort.question: When use insertion sort?
options: Small arrays (typically < 30 elements), as a base case in hybrid sorts (TimSort, IntroSort)
insertion-sort.explanation: Below ~30 elements, insertion sort beats more complex algorithms due to small constants. Many real sorts use it for small partitions.

insertion-sort.question: Insertion vs bubble sort?
options: Insertion typically faster — fewer assignments per pass and adaptive
insertion-sort.explanation: Insertion sort moves elements just enough to insert; bubble swaps repeatedly. Insertion wins in practice.

insertion-sort.question: Online algorithm property?
options: Insertion sort is online — can sort items as they arrive (one at a time)
insertion-sort.explanation: When data arrives streaming, insertion sort just inserts each new element. Most other sorts need the full input upfront.

insertion-sort.question: Insertion sort recurrence?
insertion-sort.explanation: Each insertion costs up to n shifts. Sum 1+2+...+n = n(n+1)/2 = O(n²).

insertion-sort.question: Variation of insertion sort?
options: Binary insertion sort uses binary search to find insertion point — O(n log n) comparisons but still O(n²) shifts
insertion-sort.explanation: Reduces comparisons but moves are still linear. Useful when comparisons are expensive (e.g., comparing strings).

quick-sort.question: Quicksort's average complexity?
quick-sort.explanation: Pick pivot, partition into < pivot and > pivot, recurse. Each level processes n elements. log n levels on average → O(n log n).

quick-sort.question: Quicksort's worst case?
options: O(n²) — already-sorted with bad pivot (always smallest/largest)
quick-sort.explanation: Bad pivots create unbalanced partitions: one side empty, other size n-1. Mitigated with randomized or median-of-three pivots.

quick-sort.question: Quicksort's space?
options: O(log n) average for recursion stack; O(n) worst case
quick-sort.explanation: In-place partition uses O(1) extra; recursion stack adds O(log n). Tail-call optimization keeps the deeper side iterative.

quick-sort.question: Is quicksort stable?
options: No (in typical implementation) — equal elements can be reordered during partition
quick-sort.explanation: Stable variants exist but use extra space. For most practical needs, mergesort or TimSort fills the stable role.

quick-sort.question: What's median-of-three pivot?
options: Choose median of first/middle/last as pivot — better than first or random for many inputs
quick-sort.explanation: Good defense against adversarial inputs (already-sorted, reverse-sorted). C++ std::sort uses introsort with median-of-three pivots.

quick-sort.question: Lomuto vs Hoare partition?
options: Lomuto: simpler, one pointer; Hoare: more efficient (fewer swaps), bidirectional
quick-sort.explanation: Hoare is the original. Lomuto is taught more often (CLRS). Both work; Hoare is generally faster in practice.

quick-sort.question: What's introsort?
options: Quicksort that switches to heapsort if recursion depth exceeds 2 log n — guarantees O(n log n) worst case
quick-sort.explanation: Used in C++ STL. Combines quicksort's speed with heapsort's worst-case guarantee. Best of both worlds.

quick-sort.question: Why is quicksort cache-friendly?
options: Partition operates on contiguous ranges — sequential memory access patterns suit modern CPU caches
quick-sort.explanation: Sequential reads/writes to nearby memory hit cache lines. Quicksort beats mergesort in practice partly due to this.

quick-sort.question: Tail-recursive quicksort optimization?
options: Recurse on the smaller side, iterate on the larger — bounds stack depth at O(log n)
quick-sort.explanation: Limits worst-case stack to logarithmic. Important defense against pathological inputs.

quick-sort.question: Why is quicksort the default in many languages?
options: Average-case O(n log n) with low constants and excellent cache behavior — fast in practice
quick-sort.explanation: Despite O(n²) worst case, randomization and introsort variants make quicksort the practical winner for general-purpose sorting.

selection-sort.question: What's selection sort's idea?
options: Repeatedly select the minimum from the unsorted portion and swap it to the front
selection-sort.explanation: Each pass: find min in unsorted suffix, swap with first unsorted slot. Builds sorted prefix one element at a time.

selection-sort.question: Selection sort complexity?
options: O(n²) in all cases (best, average, worst)
selection-sort.explanation: Always n × n/2 comparisons regardless of input. Doesn't adapt — even sorted input takes O(n²).

selection-sort.question: Number of swaps in selection sort?
options: O(n) — at most one swap per pass
selection-sort.explanation: Where selection sort wins: minimum data movement. Useful when writes are very expensive (e.g., flash memory).

selection-sort.question: Is selection sort stable?
options: Not in standard impl — long-distance swaps can disrupt order of equal elements
selection-sort.explanation: Workaround: insert minimum instead of swapping (shift others right). Stable but more moves.

selection-sort.question: Selection sort space?
selection-sort.explanation: Sorts in place. Combined with low swap count, suits memory-constrained environments.

selection-sort.question: When is selection sort acceptable?
options: When write cost dominates read cost — flash storage, network sync minimization
selection-sort.explanation: Niche but real applications. Most code prefers stdlib hybrid sorts. Selection sort lives mainly in textbooks.

selection-sort.question: Selection vs insertion sort?
options: Insertion sort is adaptive (O(n) best case); selection always O(n²) but fewer swaps
selection-sort.explanation: Insertion sort wins on partially-sorted input. Selection sort wins when writes are extremely expensive. Typical case: insertion sort wins.

selection-sort.question: Selection sort variation: heap selection?
options: Use a heap to find min in O(log n) instead of O(n) → O(n log n) — that's heapsort
selection-sort.explanation: Heapsort is essentially selection sort with a heap data structure backing the 'find min' step. Better complexity.

selection-sort.question: Selection sort on linked list?
options: Workable but no advantage over arrays — O(n²) regardless
selection-sort.explanation: Mergesort is preferred for linked lists. Selection sort on lists is theoretical exercise.

selection-sort.question: Why teach selection sort?
options: Simple to understand and implement; baseline for comparing more advanced sorts
selection-sort.explanation: Teaches selection thinking. Real production code rarely uses it — stdlib sort is the right answer.

heap-sort.question: What's heapsort's idea?
options: Build a max-heap, then repeatedly extract max and place at end of array
heap-sort.explanation: After heapify, root is max. Swap with last unsorted slot. Restore heap. Repeat. Sorted array forms at the end.

heap-sort.question: Heapsort complexity?
options: O(n log n) — guaranteed in all cases
heap-sort.explanation: Build heap O(n). n extractions × O(log n) each = O(n log n). No worst-case degradation like quicksort.

heap-sort.question: Heapsort space?
heap-sort.explanation: Operates on input array directly. No auxiliary storage needed. Heapify and extract use array-based heap.

heap-sort.question: Is heapsort stable?
options: No — heap operations can swap equal elements
heap-sort.explanation: Stable variants are awkward. Mergesort or TimSort fill the stable + O(n log n) niche.

heap-sort.question: Build-heap complexity?
options: O(n) — sift-down from non-leaf nodes works out to linear
heap-sort.explanation: Counter-intuitive — sum of heights of all nodes in a balanced tree is O(n). Sift-up insertion would be O(n log n).

heap-sort.question: Why is heapsort cache-unfriendly?
options: Heap operations jump around the array (parent-child indices) — non-sequential access
heap-sort.explanation: Quicksort's sequential partition is much more cache-friendly. Heapsort's Big-O is the same, but real-world performance often lags.

heap-sort.question: When choose heapsort?
options: Worst-case O(n log n) needed, in-place required, no extra memory available
heap-sort.explanation: IntroSort uses heapsort as fallback for quicksort's worst case. Real-time systems may prefer heapsort's predictability.

heap-sort.question: What's a binary heap?
options: A complete binary tree (filled level by level) satisfying heap property (parent ≤/≥ children)
heap-sort.explanation: Stored as array (no pointers): parent at i, children at 2i+1, 2i+2. Compact and cache-friendly when accessed adjacently.

heap-sort.question: Push/pop on heap complexity?
options: O(log n) — sift-up/sift-down through tree height
heap-sort.explanation: Tree height is log n. Each operation walks one path. Used for priority queues underlying Dijkstra and many other algorithms.

heap-sort.question: Heapsort vs mergesort?
options: Heap: in-place, O(n log n) all cases. Merge: stable, O(n) extra space, O(n log n) all cases
heap-sort.explanation: Pick by need: stability → mergesort. Memory tight → heapsort. General purpose → quicksort/TimSort.

search-algorithms.question: When can binary search be used?
search-algorithms.explanation: Binary search relies on sorted invariant to halve the search space. Sort first if data isn't sorted (only worth it for many subsequent searches).

search-algorithms.question: Linear search complexity?
options: O(n) — walk every element until match
search-algorithms.explanation: Worst case: target absent or last. Use when data is small, unsorted, or only searched once.

search-algorithms.question: BFS vs DFS in graph search?
options: BFS finds shortest unweighted path; DFS explores deep paths first, naturally recursive
search-algorithms.explanation: BFS uses queue, DFS uses stack/recursion. Pick based on what you need: shortest path → BFS; topological/cycle detection → DFS.

search-algorithms.question: Dijkstra's algorithm finds?
options: Shortest path from source in graph with non-negative edge weights
search-algorithms.explanation: Greedy + priority queue. O((V + E) log V) with binary heap. Doesn't work with negative weights — use Bellman-Ford.

search-algorithms.question: What's A* search?
options: Best-first search using f(n) = g(n) + h(n) where h is an admissible heuristic
search-algorithms.explanation: Generalization of Dijkstra with heuristic guidance. Optimal when h is admissible (never overestimates). Used in pathfinding (games, maps).

search-algorithms.question: Hash-based search complexity?
search-algorithms.explanation: Hash maps trade memory for fast lookups. The worst case rarely happens with good hash functions.

search-algorithms.question: When is binary search NOT suitable?
options: Linked lists (no random access), unsorted data, frequent insertions disrupting sort
search-algorithms.explanation: Linked lists need O(n) traversal. Frequent inserts into sorted array are expensive. For dynamic sorted data, use BST or skip list.

search-algorithms.question: Interpolation search?
options: Like binary search but estimates position based on value distribution — O(log log n) average for uniform data
search-algorithms.explanation: Better than binary search for uniformly distributed sorted data. Worst case O(n) for non-uniform data.

search-algorithms.question: When use exponential search?
options: Unbounded sorted arrays — find approximate range first by doubling, then binary search
search-algorithms.explanation: Useful when array size unknown or very large. O(log n) for the doubling phase + O(log n) for the binary search phase.

search-algorithms.question: What's the practical message about search algorithms?
options: Choose based on data structure: sorted arrays → binary, graphs → BFS/DFS/Dijkstra, hash maps → O(1) lookup
search-algorithms.explanation: Search complexity follows from data structure choice. Pick the structure that supports the access pattern you need most often.

binary-search.question: Binary search complexity?
binary-search.explanation: Each step halves the candidate range. log₂(n) iterations to find target or determine absence.

binary-search.question: Binary search prerequisite?
options: Data must be sorted (or sortable on the search key)
binary-search.explanation: The sort lets you discard half of the candidates each step. Without sort, you can't make valid mid-comparison decisions.

binary-search.question: Common bug in binary search?
options: Off-by-one in mid calculation or boundary updates; integer overflow in mid = (low+high)/2
binary-search.explanation: Use mid = low + (high - low) / 2 to avoid overflow. Carefully decide whether high is inclusive or exclusive (then adjust loops accordingly).

binary-search.question: What's the iterative binary search structure?
options: while (low <= high) { mid = ...; if (arr[mid] == target) return; if (arr[mid] < target) low = mid+1; else high = mid-1; }
binary-search.explanation: Memorize the canonical structure. Variants for first/last occurrence change the boundary updates and continue searching after a match.

binary-search.question: First occurrence in sorted array with duplicates?
options: Modified binary search: when arr[mid] == target, continue searching the left half
binary-search.explanation: Don't return on equality — narrow toward the leftmost match. Same idea inverted for last occurrence.

binary-search.question: Binary search on rotated sorted array?
options: Possible in O(log n) by determining which half is sorted
binary-search.explanation: Classic interview problem. Compare arr[mid] with arr[low]/arr[high] to figure out which side is sorted, then check if target is in that range.

binary-search.question: Lower bound vs upper bound binary search?
options: Lower: smallest index where arr[i] ≥ target. Upper: smallest index where arr[i] > target
binary-search.explanation: C++ std::lower_bound and std::upper_bound. Powerful for range queries, counting duplicates, finding insert position.

binary-search.question: Why is binary search recursive form less common in production?
options: Iterative avoids stack overhead and is easier to debug; both are O(log n)
binary-search.explanation: Tail recursion would help but JS lacks consistent TCO. Iterative loops are clearer and stack-safe.

binary-search.question: Binary search on answer technique?
options: When valid answers form a sorted range, binary search the answer space (e.g., min/max satisfying a predicate)
binary-search.explanation: 'Smallest divisor' or 'minimum capacity' problems. Binary search on the answer range with a feasibility check at each midpoint.

binary-search.question: When binary search beats hash lookup?
options: Range queries (find all in [a,b]), ordered iteration, when memory is tight
binary-search.explanation: Hash maps don't support range queries. Sorted arrays + binary search shine for range-based access patterns.

linear-search.question: Linear search complexity?
linear-search.explanation: Worst case: target absent or last element. Best case: target first → O(1). Average for uniform target: O(n/2) = O(n).

linear-search.question: When choose linear search over binary?
options: Unsorted data, small arrays, or one-time search where sort cost isn't justified
linear-search.explanation: Sort is O(n log n). For a single search, O(n) linear is faster than O(n log n) sort + O(log n) search. Multiple searches favor sort.

linear-search.question: Best case for linear search?
options: O(1) — target is the first element
linear-search.explanation: Big-O is worst case. Best case is constant. Variable-time guarantees for real systems often look at worst case.

linear-search.question: Optimization: sentinel search?
options: Place target at end as sentinel — eliminates inner bound check, one comparison per iteration
linear-search.explanation: Mostly academic. Modern CPUs make the bound check virtually free. Branch prediction and SIMD eclipse this micro-optimization.

linear-search.question: Linear search on linked list?
linear-search.explanation: Linked lists have no random access. Linear search is the only option (besides external indexes).

linear-search.question: Parallel linear search?
options: Yes — split array across threads/processes; each searches its chunk; combine results — speedup proportional to cores
linear-search.explanation: Embarrassingly parallel for static data. SIMD instructions can also accelerate per-thread. Careful with synchronization on first-match return.

linear-search.question: Linear search vs Set.has?
options: Set.has is O(1) average; linear search is O(n) — for repeated queries on the same data, build a Set
linear-search.explanation: Building the Set is O(n). Pays off if you do many lookups. For one-off, linear is fine.

linear-search.question: Move-to-front heuristic in linear search?
options: After finding target, move it to front — speeds up subsequent searches with locality of reference
linear-search.explanation: Self-organizing list. Helps when access patterns are skewed (some items queried much more often). Trade-off: ordering changes.

linear-search.question: When can linear search be O(log n)?
options: Never — it's defined by walking each element. log behavior would require structure (sorted array, BST)
linear-search.explanation: Linear search has no structure to exploit. Logarithmic behavior comes from data structures: sorted arrays (binary search), trees, skip lists.

linear-search.question: What's a key insight about linear search?
options: Despite simple complexity, it's the right choice for small, unsorted, or rarely-searched data
linear-search.explanation: Engineering judgment: don't reach for fancy structures when n is small. Linear search is simple, cache-friendly, and often fast enough.

tree-data-structures.question: What's a tree?
options: A connected acyclic graph with one root and parent-child relationships
tree-data-structures.explanation: Trees are hierarchical. Each node has one parent (except root) and 0+ children. Used for filesystems, DOMs, ASTs, organization charts.

tree-data-structures.question: What's a binary search tree (BST)?
options: A binary tree where left subtree values < node < right subtree values — supports O(log n) ordered ops if balanced
tree-data-structures.explanation: Insert, search, delete in O(log n) for balanced BSTs. Unbalanced (worst case: linked list shape) → O(n).

tree-data-structures.question: Why use a balanced tree (AVL, red-black)?
options: Maintains O(log n) height — guarantees logarithmic operations regardless of insertion order
tree-data-structures.explanation: Self-balancing trees rebalance via rotations on insert/delete. Trade balance maintenance work for guaranteed query performance.

tree-data-structures.question: What's a heap?
options: Complete tree with heap property (parent ≤/≥ children) — used for priority queues
tree-data-structures.explanation: Stored as array — children at 2i+1, 2i+2. Used in heapsort and priority queues. Min-heap or max-heap based on comparison.

tree-data-structures.question: Trie data structure?
options: A tree storing strings character by character — supports prefix-based queries efficiently
tree-data-structures.explanation: Used for autocomplete, spell-check, IP routing. Each path from root to leaf represents a string. Storage trade-off vs speed.

tree-data-structures.question: B-tree vs binary tree?
options: B-trees have many children per node (high fan-out); designed for disk/database to minimize I/O
tree-data-structures.explanation: Database indexes use B-trees (or B+ trees). Each node fits in a disk page. Far fewer levels for huge data → fewer disk reads.

tree-data-structures.question: Tree height vs depth?
options: Depth: root to node distance. Height: node to deepest leaf distance
tree-data-structures.explanation: Tree height = root's height = max depth across leaves. Important for analyzing balanced vs unbalanced.

tree-data-structures.question: Operations on a balanced BST complexity?
options: O(log n) for insert, delete, search, min, max, predecessor, successor
tree-data-structures.explanation: Powerful. Balanced trees give ordered iteration, range queries, and O(log n) ops — features hash maps don't have.

tree-data-structures.question: Why JS lacks a built-in balanced tree?
options: Historical — Map covers most needs; libraries (sorted-array-set, js-sdsl) provide trees if needed
tree-data-structures.explanation: Java has TreeMap, C++ has std::map, Python has sortedcontainers. JS users typically use Maps + occasional library.

tree-data-structures.question: When pick tree over hash map?
options: Need ordered iteration, range queries, predecessor/successor, or sorted output as a side effect
tree-data-structures.explanation: Hash maps win on raw speed; trees win on ordered access patterns. Pick by what queries you'll run most often.

binary-trees.question: What's a binary tree?
options: Each node has at most two children (left, right) — basis for many tree variants
binary-trees.explanation: Binary trees are the foundation. BSTs add ordering. Heaps add a heap property. Tries use them for prefix structures.

binary-trees.question: Full vs complete binary tree?
options: Full: every internal node has 2 children. Complete: filled level-by-level, last level may have gaps to the right
binary-trees.explanation: Heaps are complete (array-storable). Full trees power some classic structures (perfect binary tree).

binary-trees.question: Binary tree node structure in JS?
options: { val, left, right } — recursive object with optional children
binary-trees.explanation: Common interview pattern. Many problems involve traversing or transforming this structure.

binary-trees.question: Maximum number of nodes at depth d?
binary-trees.explanation: Each level can have double the nodes of the previous. A tree of depth d has at most 2^(d+1) - 1 nodes total.

binary-trees.question: What's the height of a binary tree?
options: Number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path
binary-trees.explanation: Height = max(left subtree height, right subtree height) + 1. O(n) worst case (skewed tree); O(log n) for balanced.

binary-trees.question: Inverting a binary tree?
options: Recursively swap left and right subtrees at each node — classic interview problem
binary-trees.explanation: Made famous by Max Howell's tweet: 'Google: 90% of our engineers use the software you wrote (Homebrew), but you can't invert a binary tree on a whiteboard so f off.'

binary-trees.question: Complete binary tree's array representation?
options: Parent at i, children at 2i+1 and 2i+2 — 0-indexed array
binary-trees.explanation: Binary heaps exploit this: no pointers, just integer indexing. Compact and cache-friendly.

binary-trees.question: Minimum height of binary tree with n nodes?
binary-trees.explanation: n nodes can fit in depth log₂(n) when balanced. Maximum height is n-1 (degenerate skewed tree).

binary-trees.question: Binary tree symmetry check?
options: Recursively check: left subtree mirror of right subtree — left.left == right.right and left.right == right.left
binary-trees.explanation: Classic recursive solution. Each pair compared simultaneously. O(n) time, O(h) recursion stack.

binary-trees.question: Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA)?
options: Lowest node that has both target nodes as descendants — important for many tree problems
binary-trees.explanation: Recursive solution: if root matches either target or both subtrees return non-null, root is LCA. O(n) time.

tree-traversal.question: What are the three DFS traversals?
options: Preorder, inorder, postorder — defined by when you visit the root relative to subtrees
tree-traversal.explanation: Preorder: root, L, R. Inorder: L, root, R. Postorder: L, R, root. Inorder of BST gives sorted order.

tree-traversal.question: What's BFS in a tree?
options: Breadth-first / level-order — visit all nodes at depth 0, then depth 1, etc.
tree-traversal.explanation: Uses a queue. Iterate: dequeue, visit, enqueue children. Used for shortest path in unweighted graphs and level-by-level processing.

tree-traversal.question: Which traversal of BST gives sorted order?
tree-traversal.explanation: BST property + inorder visits values in ascending order. Useful for printing, finding kth smallest, validating BST.

tree-traversal.question: Recursive vs iterative DFS?
options: Recursive uses call stack; iterative uses explicit stack — both O(n) time, O(h) space
tree-traversal.explanation: Recursive is concise; iterative is stack-overflow-safe for very deep trees. Convert via explicit Stack with state push/pop.

tree-traversal.question: Morris traversal?
options: O(1) space inorder traversal using temporary 'threads' (links from rightmost predecessor back to current)
tree-traversal.explanation: Modifies tree temporarily to avoid auxiliary stack. Restores structure after each visit. Niche but elegant for tight memory.

tree-traversal.question: Level-order traversal complexity?
options: O(n) time, O(w) space where w is max width
tree-traversal.explanation: Each node enqueued and dequeued once. Width can be up to n/2 for complete binary trees — significant memory.

tree-traversal.question: Preorder traversal example use?
options: Tree serialization, copying a tree, prefix expression evaluation
tree-traversal.explanation: Visiting root first lets you reconstruct or process the tree top-down. Symmetric: postorder useful for deletion or postfix evaluation.

tree-traversal.question: What's iterative deepening?
options: Run DFS with depth limit 1, then 2, then 3, ... — combines BFS's optimality with DFS's space efficiency
tree-traversal.explanation: Used in AI search (chess engines). Less memory than full BFS, finds shortest path like BFS, simple to implement.

tree-traversal.question: Postorder use case?
options: Tree deletion (delete children before parent), summing subtree values, expression tree evaluation
tree-traversal.explanation: When you need to process descendants first. Canonical example: deleting a tree without losing references mid-process.

tree-traversal.question: Why does inorder traversal of BST yield sorted output?
options: BST property: all values in left subtree < node < all values in right subtree — inorder visits in this exact order
tree-traversal.explanation: Direct consequence of BST invariant + inorder visit pattern. This property powers many BST-based algorithms.

problem-solving-techniques.question: What's the 'two pointer' technique?
options: Use two indices into one or two arrays — often slow/fast or left/right
problem-solving-techniques.explanation: Reduces O(n²) brute force to O(n) for many array problems. Reverse, palindrome, two-sum on sorted, remove duplicates.

problem-solving-techniques.question: Sliding window pattern?
options: Maintain a contiguous window in an array, expanding/shrinking based on conditions
problem-solving-techniques.explanation: Solves substring/subarray problems in O(n). Classic: longest substring without repeating chars, max sum subarray of size k.

problem-solving-techniques.question: Divide and conquer?
options: Split problem into smaller subproblems, solve recursively, combine results — basis of mergesort, FFT
problem-solving-techniques.explanation: Most efficient when subproblems don't overlap (otherwise use DP). Master Theorem analyzes complexity of D&C recurrences.

problem-solving-techniques.question: Dynamic programming?
options: Solve overlapping subproblems by storing their results — top-down memoization or bottom-up tabulation
problem-solving-techniques.explanation: Three signs: optimal substructure, overlapping subproblems, can define states. Transforms exponential into polynomial.

problem-solving-techniques.question: Greedy algorithm?
options: Make locally optimal choice at each step — works for problems with greedy-choice property and optimal substructure
problem-solving-techniques.explanation: Faster than DP when applicable but not always optimal. Examples: interval scheduling, Huffman coding, minimum spanning tree.

problem-solving-techniques.question: Backtracking?
options: Build a candidate solution incrementally; abandon ('backtrack') paths that violate constraints
problem-solving-techniques.explanation: Used for combinatorial problems: N-queens, sudoku, permutations, subset sums. Pruning is crucial for performance.

problem-solving-techniques.question: What's the key to recognizing patterns in interview problems?
options: Practice and reflect — note recurring shapes (sorted? sum? subarray? graph? tree?)
problem-solving-techniques.explanation: Solving 100+ problems builds pattern recognition. Categorize by technique. Recognize 'this is a sliding window problem' fast.

problem-solving-techniques.question: When choose recursion over iteration?
options: When problem has natural recursive structure (trees, divide-and-conquer, backtracking) and stack depth is safe
problem-solving-techniques.explanation: Recursion is clearer for tree/graph traversal and DnC. Iteration is safer for very deep recursion (stack overflow).

problem-solving-techniques.question: Hash maps as a problem-solving tool?
options: Often turns O(n²) brute force into O(n) — count, deduplicate, lookup-by-key patterns
problem-solving-techniques.explanation: Two-sum, group anagrams, valid sudoku, longest substring — hash maps are everywhere in interview solutions.

problem-solving-techniques.question: What's the best strategy for solving unfamiliar problems?
options: Restate, try small examples, identify constraints/patterns, brute force first, then optimize, finally implement
problem-solving-techniques.explanation: Don't dive into code. Discuss patterns. Sketch algorithm. Verify on examples. Talk through trade-offs. Then code.

dynamic-programming.question: What signals a DP problem?
options: Optimal substructure + overlapping subproblems + 'find min/max/count of...' phrasing
dynamic-programming.explanation: If solving subproblems separately wastes work, and the answer combines subanswers, DP applies. Classic: Fibonacci, knapsack, edit distance.

dynamic-programming.question: Memoization vs tabulation?
options: Memoization: top-down recursion + cache. Tabulation: bottom-up iterative table fill
dynamic-programming.explanation: Memoization is closer to recursive thinking. Tabulation often has lower constant factors and avoids stack overflow.

dynamic-programming.question: DP state definition?
options: Variables describing a subproblem's input — dp[i][j] often represents 'best for first i items with capacity j'
dynamic-programming.explanation: Defining the right state is the hardest part. Once state is right, transitions usually fall out naturally.

dynamic-programming.question: Knapsack problem complexity?
options: O(nW) where W is capacity — pseudo-polynomial (W can be exponential in input size)
dynamic-programming.explanation: Classic 0/1 knapsack DP. Brute force is O(2ⁿ); DP gives polynomial in n and W. For huge W, branch-and-bound or approximation.

dynamic-programming.question: Longest Common Subsequence (LCS) DP?
options: O(nm) time and space (can be optimized to O(min(n,m)) space)
dynamic-programming.explanation: Build dp[i][j] = LCS length for first i and j characters. Two strings of length 1000 each → 1M cells.

dynamic-programming.question: Edit distance (Levenshtein) DP?
dynamic-programming.explanation: Used in spell-check, DNA alignment. Classic 2D DP. Each cell considers three transitions: insert, delete, replace.

dynamic-programming.question: Space optimization in DP?
options: Often you only need the previous row/column — reduce O(nm) space to O(n) or O(m)
dynamic-programming.explanation: Many 2D DPs compute dp[i][j] from dp[i-1][...]. Two rolling rows suffice. Shrinks memory drastically.

dynamic-programming.question: When is greedy faster than DP?
options: When the problem has greedy-choice property — local optimal leads to global optimal (e.g., interval scheduling)
dynamic-programming.explanation: Greedy doesn't always work. Activity selection: greedy works. Coin change with arbitrary denominations: greedy fails, DP needed.

dynamic-programming.question: What's a state machine DP?
options: States represent positions in a finite state machine — used for stock trading problems, grouped string parsing
dynamic-programming.explanation: Examples: 'Best time to buy/sell stock with cooldown'. States: holding, sold, cooldown. Transitions defined by allowed moves.

dynamic-programming.question: DP problem-solving steps?
options: Identify state, define recurrence, base cases, then top-down or bottom-up implementation
dynamic-programming.explanation: Verbal walkthrough first: 'state is dp[i][j]', 'transition is...'. Then code. Test on small cases. Optimize space last if needed.

platforms-to-practice.question: Which platform is most popular for FAANG interview prep?
options: LeetCode — extensive problem library, company-tagged questions, mock interviews
platforms-to-practice.explanation: LeetCode dominates. Strong community, editorial solutions, contest history. Many companies pull questions directly from LC.

platforms-to-practice.question: What does HackerRank emphasize?
options: Wide skill assessments — algorithms, SQL, language-specific tracks, certification
platforms-to-practice.explanation: Used by many companies for technical screening. Practice mode covers similar problems. Less interview-style than LeetCode.

platforms-to-practice.question: What's Codeforces good for?
options: Competitive programming — timed contests, ELO rating, problems requiring clever insights
platforms-to-practice.explanation: More math-heavy and algorithmic than typical interviews. Builds raw problem-solving speed; valuable but different from interview prep.

platforms-to-practice.question: AtCoder?
options: Japanese competitive programming platform, known for clean problem statements and beginner contests
platforms-to-practice.explanation: Beginner Contest (ABC) is approachable. Higher-tier contests are very challenging. Excellent for problem variety.

platforms-to-practice.question: InterviewBit / NeetCode?
options: Curated learning paths with problems organized by topic and company — guided alternative to LeetCode's vast library
platforms-to-practice.explanation: NeetCode 75/150 list is famous: hand-picked problems covering essential patterns. Excellent for focused prep.

platforms-to-practice.question: Edabit?
options: Microchallenge platform — short problems for daily practice, more entry-level
platforms-to-practice.explanation: Good for warming up or beginners. Less FAANG-prep, more language fluency. Use as a complement to LC for daily reps.

platforms-to-practice.question: How many problems should you practice for senior interviews?
platforms-to-practice.explanation: Quality over quantity. Solve, understand the pattern, revisit a week later. Coverage of major patterns matters more than count.

platforms-to-practice.question: Should you read solutions before solving?
options: Try first, time-box (e.g., 30-45 min), then read editorial if stuck — learning patterns is the goal
platforms-to-practice.explanation: Don't grind for hours on one problem. Time-box, learn the technique, move on. Revisit later to confirm understanding.

platforms-to-practice.question: What about system design platforms?
options: Different specialty: Educative.io, GrokkingTheSystemDesignInterview, ByteByteGo for senior+ system design prep
platforms-to-practice.explanation: Mid-to-senior interviews increasingly include system design. Different skill set — distributed systems, trade-offs, capacity estimation.

platforms-to-practice.question: What's the most important practice habit?
options: Spaced repetition — revisit problems weekly; pattern recognition develops with deliberate review
platforms-to-practice.explanation: Solving once isn't enough. Schedule reviews. Use lists like NeetCode 75 with revisit dates. Active recall beats passive reading.

leetcode.question: What's LeetCode's difficulty distribution?
options: Easy, Medium, Hard — most companies focus interviews on Medium-level
leetcode.explanation: Easy: warm-up. Medium: bread and butter — what FAANG asks. Hard: stretch goals or advanced positions. Aim to solve Mediums comfortably.

leetcode.question: What's the LeetCode 75 list?
options: A curated list of 75 problems covering essential patterns — popular as a focused prep starter
leetcode.explanation: NeetCode and others maintain similar curated lists. Hand-picked to teach patterns efficiently. Better than randomly grinding.

leetcode.question: How are LeetCode problems tagged?
options: Company, difficulty, topic — useful for filtering practice
leetcode.explanation: Filter by company (Google, Meta, Amazon) and topic (DP, graph, two-pointer). Premium subscription unlocks deeper company-specific tags.

leetcode.question: What's the value of LeetCode's editorial solutions?
options: Often multiple approaches with complexity analysis — read after attempting to learn techniques
leetcode.explanation: Editorials explain why an approach works. Compare to your solution. Identify what you missed. Build vocabulary of patterns.

leetcode.question: Should you do LeetCode contests?
options: Yes — timed pressure simulates interviews, contest problems often test new patterns
leetcode.explanation: Weekly and biweekly contests. Rating gives benchmark. Live problem-solving under pressure is great training.

leetcode.question: How many LeetCode problems for FAANG prep?
leetcode.explanation: Focus on patterns. NeetCode 75 → 150 → company-tagged. Track progress. Revisit difficult ones.

leetcode.question: LeetCode Premium — worth it?
options: For active job seekers: yes — company-tagged questions, mock interviews, premium problems
leetcode.explanation: If you're prepping for specific companies, premium pays off. Free tier still has plenty for general practice.

leetcode.question: What's the LeetCode discuss tab good for?
options: User-submitted solutions, discussions, alternative approaches in many languages
leetcode.explanation: After solving, browse discuss for elegant solutions. Often you'll find a one-liner that teaches a technique. Don't visit before attempting.

leetcode.question: LeetCode beats 99% — meaningful?
options: Not really — runtime varies; beating others depends on platform load. Focus on Big-O, not 'beats X%'
leetcode.explanation: Two correct O(n) solutions can vary dramatically based on when you submitted. Optimize complexity, not percentile rank.

leetcode.question: Top LeetCode tip?
options: Solve, understand WHY the solution works, then revisit the problem weekly until pattern is automatic
leetcode.explanation: Spaced repetition + active recall. Don't 'do' problems — learn them. After 30-50 well-understood Mediums, you'll see patterns everywhere.

edabit.question: What's Edabit?
options: A platform offering small coding challenges — bite-sized practice for language fluency
edabit.explanation: Edabit's challenges are typically shorter than LeetCode. Good for quick reps and warming up.

edabit.question: Edabit difficulty levels?
options: Very Easy, Easy, Medium, Hard, Very Hard, Expert
edabit.explanation: Wide spectrum from intro syntax to genuine challenges. Beginners can build momentum; experienced devs can push themselves.

edabit.question: Edabit vs LeetCode focus?
options: Edabit emphasizes language fluency and small problems; LeetCode focuses on algorithm interview prep
edabit.explanation: Different goals. Edabit is great for warming up daily or learning a new language. LeetCode for serious interview prep.

edabit.question: Languages supported on Edabit?
options: JavaScript, Python, Ruby, Java, C#, PHP, Swift, Rust, more
edabit.explanation: Multi-language support makes it useful for trying out a new language without setting up a local environment.

edabit.question: Should you replace LeetCode with Edabit?
options: No — they complement each other. Use Edabit for warm-ups; LeetCode for interview-style prep
edabit.explanation: Different strengths. Edabit's microchallenges build syntax fluency; LeetCode's interview-style problems build pattern recognition.

edabit.question: How long is a typical Edabit problem?
options: 5-15 minutes for most levels — quick wins
edabit.explanation: Short feedback loops. Useful for daily streaks or mental warm-up before bigger problems.

edabit.question: Edabit's strength for beginners?
options: Lots of Very Easy problems to build confidence and practice syntax
edabit.explanation: Many platforms intimidate beginners. Edabit's gentle ramp helps newcomers practice without despair.

edabit.question: When pick Edabit over Codewars?
options: Personal preference — both have similar models. Try both, pick the UI/community you prefer
edabit.explanation: Codewars has a kata system, Edabit has 'challenges'. Both teach similar things. Use whichever motivates you to practice daily.

edabit.question: Are Edabit problems asked in real interviews?
options: Generally no — companies tend to use LeetCode-style problems; Edabit builds underlying skills
edabit.explanation: Use Edabit for skills, LeetCode for interview-pattern recognition. Both valuable; complement each other.

edabit.question: Long-term advice for DSA platforms?
options: Mix daily microchallenges (Edabit/Codewars) + serious LeetCode prep + occasional Codeforces contest
